title: New Zealand election 2026 live results: National and Labour neck-and-neck as minor party eyes kingmaker role
author: Mark Saunokonoko
text:
Luxon arrived to a crowd of about 700 raucous supporters chanting “three more years”. He was flanked by his wife Amanda and two children, waved and grinned as he descended a stairwell flanked in blue light.

A heavy music track - which could not be immediately identified through Shazam - thrummed as he walked down a long aisle, hugging supporters.

When he took the podium, Luxon conceded the election was “too close to call” but the crowd cheered as he announced National had secured the highest party count.

He went on to acknowledge Labour leader Chris Hipkins , and admonished supporters who booed Quilae Wong and Opportunity , saying it was “not the kiwi way”.

title: Ocon axing ‘surprised everybody at Haas’
‘Very strange, very sad’: Paraguay bank collapse fells a presidency and leaves millions broke
author: Tiago Rogero South America correspondent
text:
Santiago Peña’s links to Ueno Bank scrutinized after crisis led to his house arrest and froze millions of bank accounts

Pedro Volpe had just woken up last Tuesday when he saw a message from a friend asking whether his bank account was down, too.

It was a day after payday, and Volpe, 50, a writer and lawyer, opened his banking app and panicked: he could not even see his balance.

Volpe was among nearly 3 million Paraguayans, about 60% of the country’s adult population, whose accounts had been frozen overnight. All were customers of Ueno Bank, a digital lender that aggressively expanded across the South American country in recent years, and which, on Monday night, the central bank ordered into resolution over insolvency.

Ueno is at the centre of a political and economic crisis that has brought Paraguay’s banking system to the brink of collapse. On Friday, it led to the impeachment and house arrest of the rightwing president, Santiago Peña.

Peña had resigned the day before in a vain attempt to retain the special jurisdiction afforded to former presidents – who, under the constitution, become senators for life. Lawmakers stripped him of the seat anyway, meaning Peña will face criminal proceedings in the ordinary courts.

In just a few days, he went from being a market favourite among Latin American presidents and one of Donald Trump’s key allies in the region to facing fierce mass protests, being voted out and placed under house arrest.

The now former president is the subject of an investigation by the public prosecutor’s office over alleged favouritism towards Ueno, which, in just a few years since Peña took office in 2023, went from an obscure digital lender to the bank of choice for most Paraguayans.

“It was very easy to use and to open an account,” said Volpe, recalling that everything could be done quickly on a mobile phone. The bank also offered far more generous investment returns than its competitors did.

“Now I’m having to work miracles to pay my bills,” added Volpe. “A lot of people can’t even afford basic everyday things like food; luckily, I still had some money saved elsewhere, but that has only got me this far. I don’t know what I’ll do next week.”

Ueno was so popular – sponsoring the national football team, the league and the country’s biggest football clubs – and served such a large share of the population that businesses have already reported an overall fall in sales of up to 80% this week. Media outlets belonging to the same financial group as the bank had their operations suspended, including radio stations and the century-old newspaper La Tribuna .

The impact on ordinary Paraguayans was perhaps even wider reaching. The media freeze saw 300 workers having their salaries suspended, initially for 90 days. About 32,000 pensioners whose public pension funds had been invested in the bank were left without payments.

“A lot of people are also not working because they can’t get paid or make payments,” said the historian and political analyst Fabián Chamorro. “Meanwhile, the protests were growing every day, and Peña’s impeachment was the way congress found to prevent a popular explosion.”

A former finance minister and ex-employee of the central bank and the International Monetary Fund, Peña was elected by promising to restore a “great Paraguay” and attract foreign investment.

Soon after taking office at age 44 as the youngest president in Paraguay’s democratic history, he appointed Carlos Carvallo Spalding, who had until then been Ueno’s CEO, to lead the central bank. Less than three months later, Spalding authorised Ueno, then a finance company, to become a digital bank.

Peña himself had about $1m in shares he bought in 2019 in a company that would become Ueno Holding in 2022, the parent company of the conglomerate that controlled Ueno Bank. Even after becoming president, he only disposed of the shares in April 2025. He said he had bought them purely as an “investor”.

“During Peña’s administration, Ueno began receiving various benefits, and the government relaxed the rules to allow public funds to be invested in the bank,” said Chamorro. An estimated $800m to $860m in state and pension funds were invested in Ueno.

A series of internal central bank reports pointing to irregularities – including loans to companies within the same group – were revealed by local media in recent months, but Peña dismissed them as a “false media campaign” against his government.

With the bank having less than half the solvency required to meet its obligations, the central bank ordered it into resolution only after mounting pressure from other banks and opposition lawmakers.

Spalding resigned and, like Peña, was ordered arrested on Friday night. During the week, police had already arrested eight senior executives and directors of Ueno and its controlling group on suspicion of concealing the bank’s deteriorating financial position for months.

The public prosecutor’s office is investigating Peña on suspicion of illicit enrichment, money laundering and influence peddling. He denies all the allegations, and his lawyers said there is no evidence he directed the allocation of pension funds to the bank.

Meanwhile, most affected people still have no access to their own money.

A guarantee fund covers deposits of up to $38,000, which would apply to more than 90% of individual account holders. On Friday, the central bank began making payments to customers with up to $1,565, no outstanding debts and an existing account at another institution.

Paola Benítez, a 25-year-old chef from the capital, Asunción, met all three requirements, but by late Friday afternoon had not yet recovered the money she had been saving for her wedding.

“This has made me a bit anxious, a bit desperate too, because honestly, who am I supposed to go to and ask about this? It’s very strange, very confusing, very sad,” she said.

title: Job cuts, lost customers and a £22bn debt pile: what has gone wrong at Virgin Media O2?
author: Mark Sweney
text:
The company has lost 182,000 broadband and 644,000 mobile customers in two years and is operating in an increasingly competitive market competition

M ike Fries may be totting up swingeing job cuts, a £22bn debt pile and the loss of hundreds of thousands of customers, but he appears to be putting a brave face on the situation. “In our minds, anyway, this is not a crisis,” the boss of the co-owner of Virgin Media O2 said this week.

The UK telecoms company, which offers broadband, TV, landline and mobile services, had just announced £800m in cost savings, including potentially cutting up to a quarter of staff. Fries, the chief executive of Liberty Global , faced searching questions on its future and a potential refinancing of its huge debt pile next year. “We made it clear, we have nothing to add to where we sit today,” he said.

However, for the company’s 16,000 UK staff, the job cuts, and a raft of other measures including abandoning investing in upgrading its cable network to full fibre, are symptomatic of a business if not in crisis, then under extreme pressure. And it has left industry watchers wondering: what has gone wrong at Virgin Media O2 ?

Five years ago, Virgin Media-owner Liberty Global and Telefónica, owner of mobile network O2, completed a £31bn mega-merger that paved the way for a new “national champion” to challenge BT. It represented the latest upheaval for a company defined by a deal to bring together cable firms NTL and Telewest with Sir Richard Branson’s Virgin Mobile for a 2007 rebrand .

The post-merger mission, however, has proved tougher than bullish management, led by Fries’s lieutenant, Lutz Schüler, perhaps expected.

In the last two years the company has lost 182,000 broadband and 644,000 mobile customers, although overall numbers still remain up since the merger, according to Enders Analysis.

VMO2 is operating in a market that has seen an explosion of competition including the emergence of about 100 so-called alt-nets laying fibre networks, and BT’s belated decision to “build like fury” to replace its ageing copper lines. This fight for customers has kept prices low and put profitability and revenues under pressure.

“There are challenges everywhere in telecoms, but at VMO2 a lot of the problems boil down to operational execution,” says one senior industry executive. “ They once used Usain Bolt in ads to trumpet that they had the fastest speed broadband, now the cables they have in the ground are slower than competitors.

“Marketing, pricing, customer service, IT, billing, set top boxes, you name it and they have just not been good at executing on strategy. Yes, it is a highly competitive industry but there has been a major executional problem.”

In July, Virgin Media was fined a record £28m by telecoms regulator Ofcom after an investigation found millions of calls made by customers between January 2022 and September 2024 were probably mishandled.

The investigation showed that Virgin Media, which has repeatedly been among Ofcom’s most complained about companies in its quarterly reports, used deliberate tactics to repeatedly prevent customers from cancelling their contracts and moving to a new supplier.

Last year, its O2 mobile arm prompted a backlash after implementing a surprise monthly bill increase, 40% higher than customers had been informed when they signed up to their contracts.

Schüler later admitted that the move, which he estimated resulted in the loss of about 110,000 customers and a rebuke from the then-chancellor, Rachel Reeves, “wasn’t the best decision” .

A pledge to focus on improving customer service , and developments including a new voice AI agent to handle broadband fault calls, has paid off.

In its results earlier this week, the company pointed to Ofcom’s latest data showing significant reductions in complaints across its business, and the lowest of any leading broadband provider.

Some industry sources argue the management style since the creation of VMO2 has had echoes of hard-nosed private equity tactics – £5bn has been paid to shareholders in dividends since the merger, according to filings. Those funds could have been ploughed into fixing problems, they say.

On the call with analysts this week, Fries pointed to the importance and focus of the UK operation’s management team who were “making extraordinary efforts to bring meaningful operating free cashflow to the business”.

VMO2, which has invested £11bn in the UK since the merger, is expected to make £200m in free cashflow this year, and has significantly boosted profit margins from about 34% to just over 40% since the merger.

Some analysts believe the timing of the cost-savings announcements, which also includes a potential deal with BT to use Openreach to extend its footprint from 19m to up to 25m homes, at least in part relates to VMO2’s outrage at recent decisions relating to deals in the sector.

Earlier this month, VMO2, which declined to comment for this article, lashed out at a decision to fast-track BT’s £400m rescue of TalkTalk .

At the same time, the competition regulator had signalled that it might block the £2bn takeover of the UK’s second-largest altnet, Netomnia, by Nexfibre, whose investors include Liberty Global and Telefonica, which would thwart plans to challenge Openreach.

“A number of audiences may be in mind in constructing [VMO2’s] statement,” said Karen Egan, managing director of telecoms at Enders Analysis. “The Liberty Global shareholders, the VMO2 bondholders, and those with potential influence over the Competition and Markets Authority’s decision on the Netomnia acquisition.”

While multiple sources talk of tension between VMO2’s co-owners they argue that many of the issues facing the company date back to when cable licences were first awarded in 1984.…

title: Trump may have lost but don’t bet Democrats can fix the economy
author: Eduardo Porter
text:
There’s not much they can do over the next couple of years to alleviate angry voters’ stress over prices

It was the economy, again. Although Donald Trump largely ignored it, voters’ acute concerns over the rising cost of living fuelled a political upheaval for the ages that is likely to deliver the biggest swing toward Democrats since Watergate, granting them the largest House majority in nearly four decades alongside their biggest edge in the Senate since 2008.

Still, having come to power promising to restore affordability, the new crop of Democrats are soon to discover that there is not much they can do over the next couple of years to alleviate angry voters’ stress over pricey gas and groceries, exorbitant mortgages and unaffordable healthcare.

Democrats would do well to recall that the affordability strains that helped deliver them to power are not dissimilar to those that delivered the presidency to Trump two years ago. And they could again quickly become their enemy.

“First, Americans want Washington to bring down the cost of living,” said Chuck Schumer, Senate majority leader-in-waiting. Likely House speaker Hakeem Jeffries added that “we’ve promised to fight for an affordable America, and that’s exactly what we will do”. They will soon discover the limits to their power to undo Trump’s economic blunders and steer an economy that is largely driven by forces outside their control.

Take gas prices, the single most powerful motivation for voters’ rebellion against the Republicans enabling Trump’s policy choices. Reining them in will require reaching an understanding with Iran that reopens the strait of Hormuz. Schumer thinks Democrats can achieve that. “We are going to end the war,” he said.

Trump may disagree, however. And while it is true that Congress is legally entitled to end wars – it is the only branch of government entitled to start one – it is unclear what such legal niceties might mean in practice. Republicans have controlled Congress since Trump went to war. Still, he has pursued it without asking for their approval. Democrats could now try to cut war funding, but they do not have the requisite 60 Senate votes to prevent a filibuster.

Trump’s trade war has similar characteristics. When the supreme court struck down Trump’s “national security” tariffs because they exceeded presidential authority, the administration reimposed many of them under a different statute, deploying a new, also spurious rationale. There is also little that Democrats can do to stop Trump’s war on immigration. It is fully funded and can carry on unimpeded, further disrupting construction and other immigrant-reliant industries.

Even the low-hanging fruit hangs rather high. While it may seem easy to reinstate federal subsidies for health insurance programs under the Affordable Care Act, or undo or postpone cuts to Medicaid and food stamps in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Democrats will be hard-pressed to find the money, given a budget deficit that is already running at a whopping 6% of the nation’s gross domestic product.

Just preventing further damage will be an uphill battle. A lame duck Trump who no longer feels the need to please voters is likely to give free rein to his most destructive urges. While Democrats will be able to block Trump’s new legislative proposals, they don’t have the votes to overcome presidential vetoes.

Optimists may believe that after Tuesday’s shellacking, sufficient Republicans in Congress could be convinced to buck their president’s wishes. But most of those who survived the bloodbath come from the most faithful Maga districts and states and are the least likely to abandon their leader.

The economy itself – driven almost exclusively by a frenzied artificial intelligence investment boom – is unlikely to help Democrats achieve their goal of easing voters’ economic strains.

Wall Street is already doubting that the massive investments to build data-processing centers to train powerful AI models will pay off in time to justify the money. The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index has fallen by more than 10% in the last month.

Goldman Sachs estimates that the large AI hyperscalers have raised almost $200bn in bond markets so far this year, almost twice as much as in all of 2025. Altogether, the bank added, AI-related firms have raised nearly $500bn in debt so far in 2026.

Were this bubble to pop and the funding to stop, it would likely deliver an economic downfall to beat even the Great Recession sparked by the housing bubble in 2008. When the time comes, a government hamstrung by $40tn in debt and interest rates hovering near 20-year highs will have little fiscal space to soften the blow.

Can voters’ newfound love for Democrats survive the likely turbulence ahead? Justin Wolfers, an economist at the University of Michigan who runs Platypus Economics , observes that neither the unemployment rate nor inflation are bad enough to justify Americans’ extreme pessimism about the economy. So what’s driving the sour mood ? A collapse in confidence in economic leadership.

Tuesday’s Republican bloodbath might, on its own, improve Americans’ spirits. Limited though their powers may be, Democrats will at least offer some resistance to Trump’s most destructive impulses. But the economy will likely pose a greater challenge for the new Democratic Congress than it has to the Republicans currently in charge. In two years’ time, Democrats might be facing anger over an economic scenario that has gotten palpably worse.

They might then come to embrace the limits of their power and hope voters blame the president – not Congress – for their economic unhappiness.

Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

title: Gary Anderson's verdict on McLaren's 2027-leaning upgrade
author: Gary Anderson
text:
No team wants to show its dirty washing in public, so McLaren calling its new front wing effectively a 2027 concept seems strange.

In that position, assuming the numbers on track and the simulation tools show it has potential, I’d be using it now and considering it very much a 2026 part. With (perhaps) four races remaining and roughly five months before the start of next season, I’d be learning as much as possible from it and would hopefully make a step or two as a result of it before next season kicks off.

The intersection between the mainplane and the lower foot of the endplate, highlighted with the red ellipse, is what caught my eye.

Red Bull started the season with this concept, and Mercedes and others have followed. Making it more of a single lower surface reduces the sensitivity of the endplate footplate to the track, so in high-speed corners the front of the car should produce more consistent downforce. Basically, it should feel less snatchy, making the rear of the car more stable.

The slot gap profile between the forward and central elements, highlighted with the green arrow, has also been altered.

This is in line with the profile change highlighted with the light blue arrow and the positioning of the longest chord section of the third element. With that section slightly more inboard, this will alter where the mass flow reaches the leading edge of the floor.

What confuses me a little is the change from reducing the angle of the second and third elements in straight mode to reducing only the angle of the third when straight mode is activated. It means that the front wing is less powerful in corner mode, but that comes at the expense of overall downforce.

When the wing is in cornering mode (max downforce), the low pressure on the lower surface will pull more of its airflow through the slot gap between the first and second elements. To compensate for this, McLaren has reduced the chord length of the mainplane, highlighted with the green arrow, and increased the chord length of the second element, highlighted with the light blue arrow.

Mounting the wing on the second element, as highlighted with the red ellipse is sensible with this concept as it’s the best stiffness-to-weight compromise, but only if you don’t use the mid-flap as part of the straight-line mode wing angle reduction. So perhaps that, together with the fact that the car seems to be struggling with the balance between low- to medium-speed corners and high-speed corners, has led McLaren to this concept.

There are also small additions to the rear wing trailing edge, highlighted with the green arrows. I can’t really see enough to tell if it’s a completely new package, but I’ve highlighted the small additions. These will improve the airflow on the wing’s underside, which is affected by the twin mounting pillars. A small airflow separation problem behind those mountings can very easily spread across a much wider section of the wing’s underside.McLaren has also declared a new diffuser and a re-profiled rear beam wing.

This year the beam wing has a much shorter chord than in previous seasons, but it’s still very powerful when it comes to improving the performance of the diffuser. I don’t have the visual information to go into much detail on the diffuser.

It’s basically the component that has a major influence on the overall performance of the car, so teams tend to keep these components well hidden.

"The upgrades, even though I had half and then half, and we’re going to put everything together for tomorrow, the upgrades seem to have given what we hoped for, I would say," was Lando Norris's early verdict on Friday.

"Ultimately, the upgrades are there to bring laptime and bring performance. They’re not set out just to improve handling. A perfect upgrade is one that brings laptime and at the same time brings a handling upgrade, especially with how tricky the car’s been.

"I would say maybe there’s a small change in the right direction; it seems just a little bit more straightforward to drive.

"But I don’t think we can ever judge things over just one track. But so far, for today, things have seemed a little bit more straightforward, which is a good thing."

Let’s see how it all performs when it matters on Saturday and Sunday and if McLaren keeps all these components on the car as the weekend progresses.

title: Russell Brand barrister reports himself to watchdog over clash with journalist
author: Emine Sinmaz
text:
Ian Winter KC told Rosamund Urwin of the Sunday Times, whose investigation led to Brand’s victims coming forward: ‘I hope you are pleased with yourself’

Russell Brand’s barrister has reported himself to his professional regulator after being accused of launching a tirade at a journalist shortly after the former comedian had been found guilty of rape.

Ian Winter KC “confronted” the Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin, whose investigation led to Brand’s victims coming forward, telling her: “I hope you are pleased with yourself.”

Urwin responded: “I’m pleased justice has been done,” to which Winter replied: “Well, it wasn’t. You fucked it.”

“Congratulations,” he added, in an incident that happened outside the courtroom door at Southwark crown court on Thursday afternoon, with a group of journalists watching.

In a statement issued on Friday lunchtime, Winter said he had referred himself to the Bar Standards Board, his professional regulator.

He said: “Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today’s press, I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny.

The incident happened moments after a jury had found Brand guilty of rape and three counts of sexual assault at the conclusion of a four-week trial. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault.

Brand had denied all the charges against him, and argued through his lawyer that he had been wrongly accused and was the victim of a media conspiracy.

After the trial, experts added to calls for a change in the law to ensure juries are warned against “rape myths”.

In his closing speech, Winter said none of the complainants had “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave” during their encounters with Brand.

Claire Waxman, who is the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, is seeking to update the law to ensure juries are warned against “rape myths”. She criticised “outdated and harmful assumptions” that victims must have screamed or tried to fight off their attacker.

The head of Scotland Yard, Mark Rowley, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme he supported Waxman’s call. “I think what I’ve heard reported heads towards, it’s getting very close to victim-blaming, which is something we’ve thought very hard about in policing and make sure we don’t do.

“People fall into myths about [how] a rape victim must behave in a certain way, must react in a certain way. The evidence is really clear. Some people will fight. Some people will freeze. Some people will tell people straight away. Some people bottle it up for years. There isn’t one way of reacting.” On Friday a No 10 source said the prime minister, Andy Burnham believed that Waxman’s calls should be examined.

Speaking after the trial Urwin told a Times podcast she approached Winter after the verdict because her name had been mentioned during the trial. “I thought he’s talked about me a lot, I’ll go and introduce myself and that is a legitimate thing to do,” she said. “I was surprised to be confronted and spoken to in that way.”

It is understood that several complaints have been submitted to the Bar Standards Board but the regulator said it would not “comment as to whether or not it has received any information about potential misconduct by a barrister regardless of how any information comes to our attention”.

A spokesperson said complaints were usually handled confidentially unless they resulted in a disciplinary tribunal hearing.

The comedian Katherine Ryan criticised the barrister on her podcast Telling Everybody Everything, saying: “That was so unprofessional, so inappropriate, so aggressive. Really sickening.”

Ben Taylor, the editor of the Sunday Times , defended Urwin, his newspaper’s chief news correspondent. He said: “I found what Mr Winter did quite extraordinary. I have never seen or heard of a barrister behaving in this way. There’s a really serious point here, which is that it was not Ros who found Russell Brand guilty at Southwark crown court.

“It was a jury of eight men and four women who have sat through this case. They’ve listened to the evidence, they’ve listened to the defence, and they have gone away and they’ve come back with some very considered verdicts.

“By impugning Ros’s integrity, what Mr Winter is doing, and he should really be called to account for this, he’s impugning the integrity of the entire case.

“He’s impugning the integrity of a jury … who have sat there solemnly and done their duty, and the judge who oversaw the case and everybody else involved. I think what he did was reprehensible.”

During the trial, Winter had argued that reporting of allegations against Brand by the Times, the Sunday Times and a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary had “poisoned the well”, and rendered it impossible for his client to have a fair trial.

The trial judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, dismissed an attempt by Brand to block his trial from taking place because of negative media coverage.

In a pre-trial argument, Brand, through Winter, had accused the journalists who first exposed him as a sexual predator of being “criminals”, suggesting their reporting in 2023 had made a fair trial impossible and venturing that they may have committed the crime of perverting the course of justice.

But the judge rejected that attempt to stop the trial, ruling that Brand could simply be tried by people who had not seen the previous media reporting.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts and victims should never feel as though they are the ones on trial.…

title: Lanarkshire AI datacentre to fully rely on National Grid despite renewables claim
author: Aisha Down
text:
DataVita has revised plan for Chapelhall development to be wholly powered by 1GW of renewable energy

A datacentre company that said it would power a massive AI development near Glasgow with renewable energy has admitted that the scheme will be entirely served by the National Grid .

DataVita, a key plank of the UK’s AI strategy, had promised that the Lanarkshire project would draw 1GW – the equivalent output of a small nuclear reactor, or Britain’s largest windfarm – from green sources. But when the Guardian raised questions about the pledge , it said the arrangement was “subject to final commercial agreements, planning, grid and consenting processes”.

Now, the company, which says its proposals would transform the economy of the village of Chapelhall, outside Airdrie, has quietly revised the plan. It now says the datacentres will be “fully grid served” with the possibility that solar and windfarms “could connect in the future”.

DataVita says the power it draws from the grid will be largely renewable energy. The company remains in receipt of £202m of public money in the form of wealth guarantees from Britain’s national wealth fund.

While the shift may appear to have been inevitable given the implausibility of the claimed renewables provision, it could present a problem for both DataVita and Britain’s AI strategy.

Under the former prime minister Keir Starmer, Britain’s AI strategy was to build massive datacentres in zones across the country. Their developers would get incentives – including, potentially, discounts on energy and expedited planning approvals. DataVita was to build one of the key developments associated with this strategy, an “AI growth zone” in Lanarkshire.

But this strategy began to founder just over a year after it was announced, when the Guardian’s investigations demonstrated that there was little solidity behind many announced plans.

AI datacentres are some of the most energy-intensive structures humanity has ever built, and energy costs are higher in Britain than in most of Europe. There is a years-long wait for the UK developments to connect to the grid.

Two key UK AI investments – announced with great fanfare by Starmer’s government – are on shaky ground after questions emerged over their ability to power themselves, or pay the high energy costs necessary to realise their stated ambitions. Now DataVita, which was supposed to bring 3,400 jobs to Lanarkshire by building a 500MW datacentre, also appears to be backtracking on its energy plans.

In a response to the Guardian, the company said it had not misrepresented its intention to supply renewables to the site earlier this year. “Our commitment to renewable energy is unchanged,” said a spokesperson. However, they added: “Our datacentres are being designed to be grid served … Our grid supply will be through a renewable power purchase agreement.”

This appears to contradict an earlier announcement, in which the company said: “More than 1GW of renewable energy capacity, including wind, solar, and battery storage, will be delivered through private wire connections directly linked to the datacentres.”

DataVita left open the possibility that its datacentres would connect to renewable energy in the future, through a wind and solar park it proposes to build in North Lanarkshire.

Kat Jones, the director of the Edinburgh-based charity Action to Protect Rural Scotland , said DataVita’s apparent change in direction was “emblematic of the hyperbolic claims being made by datacentre developers in Scotland”.

“Hyperscale AI datacentres simply cannot run on renewable power alone, they absolutely need a highly reliable source of grid power,” she said. “It is not surprising that the goalposts have now changed.”

title: Trump faces criticism for ‘dangerous’ Stephen Miller appointment as White House chief of staff
author: Ariana Baio in Washington
text:
Democrats and Republicans blast promotion of ‘xenophobe’ who led administration’s immigration crackdown in wake of US midterm elections

Democratic lawmakers decried Stephen Miller as a “ hatemonger ”, a “ xenophobe ” and “ vile ” after Donald Trump appointed his most trusted adviser as White House chief of staff.

On Friday afternoon, the US president abruptly announced via his Truth Social platform that Miller – the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown – would replace Susie Wiles, whom he confirmed had been ousted.

The announcement came just days after voters overwhelmingly elected Democrats in the US midterm elections, a sharp rebuke of Trump’s agenda that ended his Republican party’s control of US Congress.

“For Trump to promote this hatemonger shows he has learned nothing,” Dick Durbin, a Democratic senator from Illinois, wrote on X . Chuck Schumer , who is expected to become Senate majority leader, said Trump “learned nothing from his historic defeat” and “couldn’t have made a worse choice” in elevating Miller.

Hakeem Jeffries, the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, who is widely expected to become the chamber’s first Black speaker, called Miller “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands”, and demanded he be fired.

Chris Van Hollen , a Democratic senator from Maryland, called Trump’s decision to elevate Miller “another kick in the teeth to the American people” and “a sign of Trump’s contempt for the voters”.

Miller, who has been serving as Trump’s deputy chief of staff, has become one of the most controversial figures in the administration. An author of the rightwing Project 2025 manifesto , Miller often makes TV appearances to attack Trump’s opponents or bolster policies such as ending birthright citizenship and suggesting the US could invade Greenland .

As a policy adviser, Miller is credited as the architect of Trump’s mass deportation agenda, which Democrats pointed to in denouncing his promotion.

Gavin Newsom, the outgoing California governor, called Miller “one of the most vile thugs to ever slither into the Oval Office” and said the move was “an insult to every American who voted for change” on Tuesday.

But Trump’s Republican allies and aides celebrated the announcement. Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, called Miller a “Trump OG” , and said: “There is no bigger advocate for the Trump agenda than Stephen.”

Mike Lee, a senator from Utah, said Miller had been “a staunch defender of law and order against illegal invasions and leftist lawlessness”. Eric Schmitt, a senator from Missouri, insisted Miller was exactly what the country needed. “Our country is at a pivotal point and Stephen Miller understands exactly what is at stake,” Schmitt wrote on X .

Cabinet members including JD Vance , defense secretary Pete Hegseth , health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr and secretary of state Marco Rubio also praised Miller’s record.

Not all Republicans were pleased by the appointment, however.

Congressman Marlin Stutzman, an Indiana Republican who held his seat, argued Miller “should be fired” earlier this week amid anger over the administration’s deportation drive. Asked on Friday what he made of Trump’s choice to promote Miller instead, Stutzman told Semafor it was a “horrible decision”.

Miles Taylor, who served as chief of staff at the Department of Homeland Security during Trump’s first term, and later joined the ranks of anti-Trump Republicans, said: “I spent two years working with Stephen Miller. His appointment as White House chief of staff is among the most dangerous personnel decisions in the history of our republic. I say that without reservation.”

Asked about such criticism on Friday, the White House hailed Miller as a “key player” delivering Trump’s agenda. “He has spearheaded the administration’s crime crackdown including in DC and Memphis, record setting deregulation, unleashed American energy, dismantled drug cartels, and secured our border,” it said in a statement. “In his new role, he will continue to deliver historic successes for the American people.”

Accepting his new role, Miller thanked Trump and said he was “honored beyond words” to serve. “The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic,” Miller wrote on X .

title: The datacentre arms race hits pause in south-east Asia
author: Arundhati Hazra
text:
Power and water constraints are pressuring what seemed like a juggernaut of growth for the region just months ago

I n early 2026, Thailand’s datacentre industry was on a roll. The country’s board of investment had recently announced approval of datacentre projects from Tiktok, a UAE-based Skyline datacentre and Singapore’s Bridge datacentres, totalling a planned investment of $27bn.

As the year has passed, however, what once seemed like a new industrial juggernaut has ground to a halt. Thailand paused construction on 49 projects and approval decisions on 117 more in September 2026, amidst growing concern about the lack of sufficient details for regulation and monitoring. It is not alone in reconsidering datacentre projects. In neighbouring Indonesia, the governor of the country’s most populous province of West Java halted construction on a datacentre due to lack of permits and an incomplete environmental assessment process.

With the global rise of AI usage driving an increased demand for datacentres, south-east Asia has emerged as a surprise centre of growth in the Asia Pacific region. While China has the largest operational datacentre capacity in the region, a 2026 report by real estate firm Cushman and Wakefield shows that south-east Asia has the largest share of under-construction datacentre capacity in Asia Pacific, about 50% of the total. Malaysia and Thailand comprise a large portion of that capacity.

Through the 2010s, Singapore was south-east Asia’s leading datacentre hub, with companies like Alibaba and Facebook opening facilities there. However, the city-state implemented a moratorium on new datacentres from 2019 to 2022 because they were “intensive users of water and electricity”, as described in a press release from the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry. Since then, approval has been selective amidst land constraints and sustainability requirements, with just 95MW of operational capacity added between 2023 and 2026, per Cushman and Wakefield .

With the advent of LLMs and rise in usage of AI, associated datacentre demand has surged in the last half decade, and desperate companies looked beyond Singapore to build datacentres. Malaysia has been a major beneficiary, with operational capacity in the southern state of Johor growing more than tenfold from 94MW in 2023 to 1110MW in 2026, with 3088MW additional under construction or planned. Johor has become the largest datacentre hub in south-east Asia, attracting $40bn of datacentre investment as of 2026, according to Menteri Besar Onn Hafiz Ghazi, the head of the state government. Key operators include Microsoft, which announced a $2.2bn investment for cloud and AI infrastructure across Kuala Lumpur and Johor in 2024, and Australian datacentre company AirTrunk, which said it plans to invest $3bn to double its datacentres in Johor from two to four.

Other countries in south-east Asia are catching up. Indonesia has a datacentre development pipeline of 1699MW in greater Jakarta, and is developing the island of Batam as a secondary hub . Microsoft is building five datacentres as part of a$1.7bn investment in the country, and Singapore-based datacentre operators Princeton Digital Group and Digital Edge are also expanding. In Thailand, Bangkok’s development pipeline stands at 2084MW, while secondary markets like Manila and Ho Chi Minh City are ramping up operations, based on Cushman and Wakefield’s analysis.

While the rush to build more datacentres is attracting big investments across the region, it is putting a strain on each country’s resources. Energy consultancy Wood Mackenzie estimates that datacentres in Johor already account for 24% of the state’s total power consumption today, which could grow to 40% by 2035.

“The rapid growth of datacentre developments in Johor has the potential to create localized grid connection bottlenecks and increase the need for transmission network upgrades as well as new power supply capacity,” says Alvin Tan, research analyst at Wood Mackenzie.

Thailand’s energy minister, Akanat Promphan, has said that datacentres require large amounts of power generated from expensive imported gas, and called for a new electricity user category with higher tariffs to reflect the demand.

Datacentres’ water-guzzling tendencies are also a major cause of concern for officials in the region. Johor is prone to droughts, and the current operational datacentres are estimated to need about 675m cubic meters of water per day. In Indonesia, a report by research firm Tenggara Strategics shows that many datacentres are water-cooled and situated in hot and humid lowland environments, resulting in elevated water consumption in comparison to facilities in more favourable temperatures.

In Thailand, datacentre projects in the country’s Eastern Economic Corridor have residents concerned about the pressure on their already depleted water reservoirs.

“The Khlong Luang Reservoir in Chonburi (in eastern Thailand) is a primary flashpoint,” says Somnuck Jongmeewasin, research director of research and advocacy group EEC Watch. “Despite the reservoir being shallow and under strain, authorities are piping its water to industrial estates,” he adds.

Local communities are waking up to the changes. In February, Johor saw its first public protest against datacentre construction , with demonstrators picketing a project by China’s ZData Technologies. Protesters expressed concern about the dust pollution caused by construction of the site near a residential location and the potential impact on water supply.…

title: Home Office sued after stripping almost 1,500 EU citizens of right to live in UK
author: Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent
text:
Campaign group the3million lodges court papers after EU citizens told pre-settled status was an ‘error’

The Home Office is being sued for alleged breach of the Brexit withdrawal agreement after stripping almost 1,500 EU citizens of their full rights to live in the UK.

Campaign group the3million lodged papers at the high court on Friday after several cases emerged of EU citizens who were granted pre-settled status to remain in the country after Brexit but were told recently those decisions were an “error”.

According to the statement of claim, the Home Office decision to remove all or some rights from citizens granted pre-settled status was made without “procedural protections” required under the Brexit withdrawal agreement (WA).

These protections include a right of an appeal and an assessment of “proportionality”, which would establish whether removal of rights was appropriate given the EU citizens in question built their lives in the UK on the basis of the Home Office’s original decision.

Among the people affected by the Home Office policy was a 33-year-old Brazilian Italian engineer who has been in London since 2018. He was originally told that he should not have settled status: he could stay but his Brazilian wife could not, a decision that was reversed in the last few weeks after objections were raised.

Another EU citizen who raised her case with the3million is a woman working in the NHS and studying for a PhD in dentistry. She has said the Home Office’s notification had “turned her life upside down” .

In October 2026, the Home Office accepted that where a person provides evidence of their Italian citizenship, together with evidence that this was obtained through jure sanguinis , they would now accept that this person was an Italian from birth.

Previously it told a number of Brazilian Italians they were granted status “in error” because they had not presented an Italian passport at the time of their application, merely stating they were Italian citizens.

Monique Hawkins, acting CEO of the3million, said: “The Home Office is putting the cart before the horse. It denies people the safeguards the withdrawal agreement guarantees – a fair assessment and a right of appeal – because it says they are ‘clearly’ not covered by the agreement. That’s like saying someone doesn’t need a trial because they’re ‘clearly’ guilty.”

She said the Home Office U-turn on jure sanguinis Italian nationals showed it could change its policy when its errors were exposed.

The high court papers said: “This is a simple matter of providing proper due process. Despite our advocacy efforts since early 2025, the Home Office refused to change course, so we have no option but to challenge the policy in court.”

The campaign group is asking the court to declare that the “grant in error policy is unlawful, by breach of the WA and/or common law” and make whatever order is necessary to “excise the offending parts of the published policy”

Many complained that although they were jure sanguinis (direct and unbroken Italian relative), they could not get a passport because the public institutions were in lockdown during the coronavirus pandemic.

Lawyers have also argued that the apparent generosity of the UK, which minimised the evidence required by any EU citizens applying to stay after Brexit, “compounded” the current Home Office policy of removing rights.

The unlawfulness of the policy is compounded by the nature of the EU settlement scheme itself. The UK deliberately implemented a scheme that, in a number of respects, operated more generously than the minimum requirements of the WA.

Hawkins said: “Grants were also made through processes involving evidential flexibility and, in some cases, discretionary decision-making.

“As a result, many status holders cannot know, and are given no means of knowing, whether their status was granted because they satisfied the substantive requirements of the WA, because they satisfied the requirements of Appendix EU as a matter of domestic law, because a caseworker exercised evidential flexibility or discretion in their favour, or because the grant was genuinely erroneous.”

Several cases have come to light of Brazilians who have Italian parents or grandparents. Under Italian law these citizens are Italian by birth but the Home Office alleged they were not because they did not have an Italian passport at the time.

This is not the first time the Home Office has been sued over its implementation of the withdrawal agreement.

In 2022 it was taken to court by the statutory watchdog set up to ensure the Home Office implemented the withdrawal agreement properly.

The Independent Monitoring Authority, backed by the3million, accused the Home Office of putting EU citizens at risk of losing their rights to work or rent a home by forcing them to reapply for settled status once their pre-settled status expired.

High court judges ruled in the IMA’s favour concluding the conditions imposed by the Home Office were unlawful.

A spokesperson for the Home Office said they could not comment as proceedings were ongoing.

title: TikTok accused of helping to promote sex industry to girls
author: Amelia Gentleman
text:
Researchers say popular performers covertly market OnlyFans content and tell followers about wealthy lifestyle

TikTok is helping to promote and normalise the sex industry, allowing “sexfluencers” to post videos aimed at marketing pornographic content they have uploaded elsewhere on sites such as OnlyFans, a report indicates.

After studying non-explicit content posted on TikTok over the course of a year by some of OnlyFans’ most popular young female performers, researchers said the women buried coded references to pornography in “girly lifestyle content” that showed them shopping, playing with their pets, baking or offering skincare advice.

While mentioning OnlyFans or directly linking to OnlyFans from TikTok accounts is prohibited, euphemisms, emojis and crude gestures are used to indicate that performers’ adult content is available for sale on other platforms. TikTok prohibits sexual solicitation, including invitations to share explicit images, but the platform distributes so-called safe-for-work material produced by popular OnlyFans performers.

The report analyses how hints about adult content are hidden in widely shared TikToks that show OnlyFans stars filming their hair and makeup routine for “get ready with me” posts – known by the acronym GRWM. Performers may use the word “corn” instead of the word “porn”, or add the corn emoji next to a star emoji, to avoid the content being blocked.

The “TikTok to OnlyFans pipeline” study was conducted by researchers from the campaigning organisations Cease (Centre to End All Sexual Exploitation) in the UK and Collective Shout in Australia. Researchers spent months scrolling through posts from a number of key “sexfluencers” and then following recommendations offered up by TikTok’s algorithm.

In viral posts, OnlyFans performers told their followers on TikTok about the money they had earned from selling sexual content. “One of the most pervasive messages across these posts is that selling sexual services on OnlyFans gives you a fabulous life – a life filled with freedom, fun, friendship and lots of money,” the report states.

Many posts promoted this message with images of cash, big houses, private jets and expensive cars, beneath headlines such as “how it feels knowing I own all of this at 23 thanks to 250,000 men”.

In some posts, OnlyFans was presented as the answer to poverty and unemployment by performers who described rag-to-riches stories. Opening an OnlyFans account was marketed as a solution, “rescuing women and girls from bleak, underprivileged lives, gifting them with the nice, luxury items that they – and their struggling families – have always deserved”, the report says.

OnlyFans’ own data indicates that its top 5,000 creators have made more than $1m each on the site since the platform launched in 2016. But the average earnings of the site’s 5 million registered performers are estimated to be about $1,000 a year, the report states.

Melinda Tankard Reist, of Collective Shout, condemned TikTok as “an industrial-scale digital pimp funnelling girls into the sex industry”. She said: “It is our view that young women and girls deserve to be protected from a predatory industry grooming them to be producers of explicit content.”

Tankard Reist said the research was commissioned in response to an awareness that OnlyFans stars such as Sophie Rain and Ari Kytsya had a huge following on TikTok among teenage girls, and concern that they were using the site to promote benefits of creating pornography.

Rain became famous with content filmed in the “Bop House”, a luxury pornography production house in Miami, which is home to a rotating group of women who sell sexual content on OnlyFans. Auditions to join the Bop House are shared on TikTok and would-be recruits respond by posting sexually suggestive dances tagging Bop House recruitment.

OnlyFans performers rely on building up their followers on TikTok and other social media platforms, so they have become adept at finding ways to make subtle nods to the presence of explicit content that is for sale elsewhere. The report focuses on the ties between TikTok and OnlyFans because TikTok has such a high proportion of young users and because it is where the careers of many on OnlyFans start out.

Many OnlyFans stars do brand promotion alongside their lifestyle content on TikTok, advertising household items such as pet food, burgers and pineapple juice, as well as sex toys and condoms. The global cosmetics brand L’Oréal last year appointed Kytsya – who refers to herself as a “mattress actress” – as a brand ambassador for Urban Decay, a makeup brand popular with teenagers and sold globally. In these advertisements, viewed millions of times on TikTok, she calls for makeup that performs well on mattresses.

The report’s authors have called for an extension of the ban that exists in many countries on showing explicitly pornographic content to under-18s so that it also includes posts that promote or are related to the sex industry.

A TikTok spokesperson said: “TikTok strictly prohibits the sharing or showing of sexual content and we use advanced technologies to enforce our community guidelines. In addition, our systems are designed to prevent age-inappropriate content from reaching teens.”

An OnlyFans spokesperson said: “OnlyFans is a platform for people aged 18 and over and we have strict onboarding processes to prevent minors accessing the platform.”

title: Infantino caught in the web as tide turns against Trump in midterms and leaves Fifa exposed | Barney Ronay
author: Barney Ronay
text:
Trump Exposed Reactor Core Syndrome very much in play after Democrat landslide – and Fifa’s president may pay a price

O h baby, clamp me in your repulsive mouthparts. Sink your unusually large and venomous fangs into my abdomen. And yes, we are doing this in the White House cabinet rooms, out there in plain sight of the watching world, just a gleaming golden ball between us. But it’s fine. Probably. Now take a sip of those sweet, sweet tiny male arachnoid entrails.

An exciting new study was published over the summer into the habits of the Australian redback spider. The research made headlines for its focus on reproductive behaviour, specifically the male’s urgent and very willing engagement in what is known as sexual cannibalism , AKA copulatory suicide.

Scientists observing these tiny arachnoids discovered that during the act of lovemaking with the larger, more decorative female, the male will perform a spectacular sexual death-somersault, flipping himself upside down, presenting his underbelly to the female’s fangs, and urging her to literally consume his intestines mid-coitus as an energy snack and self-dooming sweetener. You’ve already ripped my heart out, babe. Now take my guts as well.

This doesn’t paint a very flattering picture of the male redback’s sense of himself, his ability to recognise boundaries in a relationship. Overall, the picture is of a craven, fawning, hairless entity, entirely in thrall to its power-master. Yes, it might make sense for a while to place your prospects in the hands of a glassy-eyed red-tinged predator at the heart of a toxic web of power. But it can land you in a spot of bother down the line.

In unrelated news, there was a sense this week that Gianni Infantino’s entanglements with Donald Trump may have now moved one step closer to scrutiny, sunlight, consequences, perhaps even some kind of decisive intestinal devouring. The sight of Infantino cavorting for the US president was one of the more grotesque sport-adjacent spectacles of recent times. What kind of relationship was this?

How will history remember that display of power-fluffing, the supposedly apolitical Fifa president sat nodding gravely at the walnut-veneered table as the latest immigration policy is trailed, beaming along as some random crypto-waffle is chucked into the mix, and becoming through this an ever more contorted figure, as though essence of human mendacity has been condensed, reconstituted into a fine paste, pumped into a serge blue suit and taught to walk around saying the phrase: “My magic ball unites the golden peace world.”

At the time it felt as though this was some kind of warning siren, a real-time satire on the idea of unaccountable executive power. Is this just allowed now, confirmation in human form that acting as though you exist outside the rules is halfway to actually being there?

Well, maybe not. As of Wednesday there is for the first time a sense of something potentially self-dooming about that public two-hander. Perhaps this is the best way to picture those interactions now, Infantino backflipped in supplication, thighs clamped around the presidential shoulders, presenting his tenderest parts to those razor-sharp mandibles. Feast on my entrails. Consume my borrowed sporting soul. Empower me. Or don’t. Whatever. We’ll talk later.

Trump may be heading into a diminished final two years in office. But Trump Exposed Reactor Core Syndrome is still very much in play, a principle that states, yes, he will give you heat, light and a deathly glow. But he will also melt your face in the process. And maybe this process is now finally coming for the world’s second-most-provocative elected president.

The headline Fifa news this week was the council member Kozo Tashima’s announcement that he will stand as a candidate in March’s leadership vote. There is, at the very least, someone else to vote for now. In the wider world, but potentially more significant to the Infantino regime, the US midterm elections brought a Democratic landslide in the Senate and the House of Representatives.

Football is, as ever, just a tiny notch on the to-do list. To date those results are simply a rejection of something, the chance to luxuriate in the defenestrating of some of those High Trump oddities, the senator who believes a cabal of Sikhs is trying to steal the moon, the House representative on record as saying all Eritreans are genetically derived from yoghurt, the one-term governor who looks as if he bites the heads off sparrows and wears a suit made entirely from recycled human fingernails.

What comes next is not clear. But there is talk of cleaning house. Internal judicial matters are now firmly in the hands of Trump’s opponents. Some Democrats have warned of the need to “lawyer up”, have spoken about correcting the most excessive acts of opportunism over the past two years.

Even as Infantino is out there bartering for his future, bothered at mosquito-level by a cloud of revelations – the use of Fifa resources to electioneer, talk of having his maid’s visa raised at government level – the one thing that may actually get close to him is force majeure.

At which point enter the tantalising figure of Jamie Raskin, representative for Maryland’s 8th district, and widely tipped to become the new chair of the House judiciary committee. Raskin is a hawk on what he describes as “the corruption” of aspects of the Trump regime. And these include Fifa.

Raskin’s letter to Infantino dated 26 July bears re-reading. First he brings up the wire fraud and money laundering case against Full Play Group that was part of the 2015 indictments against the Blatter regime and that was dropped by the Trump administration because it was “not a priority”.…
