title: Can AI really save you money on your heating bill? I spent two years testing to find out
author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor
text:
Samuel Gibbs doubted he could cut costs and still keep warm by putting tech in control. The results surprised him

C an smart thermostats and AI reduce your heating bills? Every manufacturer claims the answer is yes , quoting average savings in the 25%, or £180 a year range. But all of these promises are heavily caveated and, with energy costs changing regularly, it can be very difficult to tell what is having an impact.

To find out if technology can really help, I spent the last two years comparing my miserly manual control and basic heating schedule to an AI-governed system. The results surprised me.

I used my 1930s solid-brick house with a recent, insulated loft conversion as the test bed.

In the winter of 2024 my heating system consisted of a 10-year-old Worcester Bosch combination gas boiler set to a medium heat, a Hive thermostat in a central hallway with its smart features disabled and 13 radiators equipped with standard thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs).

To maximise energy savings, I set a basic schedule to turn the heating on for a couple of hours in the morning and evening, turned off the TRVs in rooms we did not use and manually adjusted those in other rooms when we did not need them to be heated. I also manually turned the heating off when leaving the house.

It was laborious and not all that comfortable at times. I frequently found myself being glared at by other members of the family who were shivering under blankets in the living room while watching The Traitors. Or being called a traitor after denying yet another request to turn up the heating. But it kept bills low throughout the winter and money in my pocket.

After controlling for hot water usage by using recordings from when the heating was not used during the summer months of 2025 to create a daily average, my manual control consumed 14,316.7 kilowatt hours of gas across 213 days from November to May. This was about 10 to 15% lower than in previous years when I had not been quite so controlling and miserly.

In the summer of 2025 I replaced the Hive thermostat with a full Tado X system connected to the existing combi boiler. This system consisted of 13 smart radiator thermostats to replace the standard TRVs, a wireless thermostat in each of the two largest rooms, and a programmer wired to the boiler.

Instead of a central thermostat and a schedule with just one temperature for the whole house, heating is managed room by room. Each smart TRV can control the temperature of an individual room by commanding the boiler to turn on and then adjusting the hot water flow into the radiator. The TRVs in rooms that don’t need heating turn the radiators off, which maximises the efficiency of the boiler as it has to burn less gas to maintain the same water temperature.

If your boiler supports the OpenTherm protocol – check your boiler’s documentation or contact the manufacturer to find out – it can also tell the boiler to turn down its flow temperature to reduce energy consumption. My boiler does not.

Tado’s smartphone app controls the lot and allows you to quickly mirror schedules across multiple rooms or get as fine-grained for each room as you like.

The system is not cheap. It costs about £930 for the full setup I tested – I was lent the equipment by Tado. It can be easily DIY installed apart from the part wired into your boiler, which costs about £80 in labour by a heating engineer.

By default, it uses push notifications to remind you to turn the heating off when you leave or if it detects an open window in a room. But for the AI-powered smarts I tested, a subscription is required, costing £3.99 a month or £29.99 a year.

This promises to further improve the system’s efficiency through automation and numerous additional features. The monthly subscription can be paused if you are not using the heating.

The AI is built by Tado using anonymised data collected from more than 1m homes, which it does not sell to third parties . It learns how quickly a room heats up and cools down and uses that information to more precisely control the temperature and energy consumption.

It also performs automatic hydronic balancing to increase efficiency, taking the guesswork out of balancing your radiators. It automatically turns off the radiators in a room when it detects an open window, turns off the heating when the last person with the Tado app on their phone leaves home and preheats your home for when it predicts you will step back in the door.

The subscription records 13 months of logs of your heating activity, rather than just the last month, and enables Tado’s energy IQ system, which shows you the overall cost of your heating down to the cost for individual rooms, helping to spot any potential for improvements in any part of your house.

Tado is the biggest manufacturer of smart heating controls in Europe, but there are alternatives with similar per-radiator control, including Hive, Drayton and Honeywell. Google’s Nest, which offered smart-learning thermostats , pulled out of Europe in 2025.

I set a schedule for when the heating would run in each room. I turned on all the AI features and recorded monthly meter readings throughout the winter of 2025 and into 2026.

In the first week, the energy IQ feature highlighted that one of my radiators consumed a lot of energy heating an uninsulated porch. Since you are barely in the porch for any time before closing the front door, it seemed a waste, so I quickly adjusted the schedule to turn it off most of the time.…

title: Early release prisoners facing street homelessness, probation staff warn
author: Jessica Murray Social affairs correspondent
text:
Charities say situation exposes ‘fatal flaw’ in Andy Burnham’s plan to end rough sleeping in England by Christmas

In just four days James is facing the prospect of sleeping on the street. He was released from prison in August and given temporary probation accommodation in Somerset, but that is about to expire and he has nowhere to go.

“It is scary,” the 37-year-old said. “I am not asking for special treatment. But literally nowhere wants to help – I have contacted MPs, solicitors, probation and the council. I am quite tempted to just get myself recalled to prison because it is November. It is cold.”

Charities and probation staff have said that prisoners are at risk of being released into street homelessness, exposing a “fatal flaw” in Andy Burnham’s plan to try to end rough sleeping in England by Christmas .

With hundreds of prisoners being released early in England and Wales to try to ease prison overcrowding, there are concerns the number sleeping rough could start to rise just as the weather turns cold.

Tania Bassett, from Napo, the trade union for probation staff, said most housing options were already full after the early release of prisoners in October, and there were major concerns about how they would house the next tranche of releases on 10 November.

“There is this juxtaposition of releasing people into homelessness at the same time as Andy Burnham is saying we’re going to solve rough sleeping,” she said. “I think there is an assumption that probation can magically bring up houses for people to move into. But there is very little available and it is a big concern for our members.”

She said one member had been trying to find housing for 10 people who were released on 1 October, and many staff reported feeling overwhelmed. Andy Keen-Downs, chief executive of the Prison Advice and Care Trust (Pact), said: “Every single day we are seeing men and women coming back to prison because they did not make their probation appointment. And when we ask why, they say, ‘Well, I was sleeping on a bit of cardboard’. That is still the daily reality.”

James said everyone he had met since living in the probation hostel had been released without an address, with many people sleeping in cars and on benches. He has a number of medical conditions, including epilepsy and PTSD, but has been denied temporary accommodation from Somerset council and has also been rejected from probation housing.

He has two electronic tags – a GPS tracker that needs to be charged daily and an alcohol monitoring tag that needs to remain connected to a communication device. “How am I supposed to comply with these requirements while sleeping rough without reliable electricity or somewhere safe to put the equipment? Nobody has given me a satisfactory answer,” he said.

The government has introduced a “presumption of electronic tagging” for offenders released early, but Bassett said this could not happen if there was a high level of homelessness.

Analysis by Pact showed the number of prisoners released into rough sleeping has increased by 130% in three years, rising from 6,040 in 2022-23 to 14,360 in 2025-26.

Rough sleeping is now recorded in about one in seven prison releases, compared with around one in 10 three years ago, and the proportion of releases recorded as “no fixed abode” (homelessness and rough sleeping combined) has risen from 11.3% to 15.9%.

Enver Solomon, CEO of the social justice charity Nacro, said he recently visited a prison that was aiming to ensure 84% of prisoners had a roof on release.

“Which effectively meant they were accepting that 16% would be homeless,” he said. “I think the government realises this is a critical part of the jigsaw, but it is taking time to work out what needs to be done to address it. And time is of the essence.”

Keen-Downs said that while Burnham’s ambitions to end rough sleeping in England and his £874m funding boost were welcome, the lack of money for post-prison support was a “fatal flaw”.

“We need more money for beds, but we also need money for all the support services people need to get from the prison cell into the bed and stay in it,” he said.

Bassett said: “If there is not any money ringfenced to help prisoners, that is a real missed opportunity to end this never-ending cycle. We will be making strong representations to the chancellor for some of that money to go towards this specific issue.”

A spokesperson for Somerset council said: “While we cannot comment on individual cases, we have a statutory duty to work with people who are homeless or at risk of homelessness to assess their circumstances, provide appropriate advice and support, and explore all suitable accommodation options for them. We are committed to ending rough sleeping in Somerset, with our aim being to prevent homelessness wherever possible.”

A government spokesperson said: “We’re working with councils and charities to tackle prison leaver homelessness, backed by record investment in probation and our drive to ensure anyone sleeping rough is offered a route off the streets or wider support by Christmas. Prison leavers can also receive support from specialist services after leaving temporary accommodation.

“We’re also training prisoners for work and partnering with hundreds of employers to help prison leavers move straight into jobs, so they can rebuild their lives and contribute to their communities.”

title: Nationwide launches savings account with ‘market leading’ 5.3% interest
author: Rupert Jones
text:
Many experts think fixed rate on 30-month term will still look good after Bank of England raised base rate

A savings account paying “market-leading” 5.3% interest was launched this week by Nationwide building society. It’s only for Nationwide members – but there are more than 19 million of them.

The account was launched just a couple of days before the Bank of England pushed up the main base rate to 4%, a move that will be welcomed by many savers.

Nationwide says the fixed-rate account is part of its commitment to reward existing members for their loyalty. The Member Exclusive Bond has a 30-month term, and you can pay in from £1 to £10,000. Someone saving the full £10,000 would receive £1,381 in interest at the end of the term.

Many experts think that 5.3% fixed rate will still look good after Thursday’s base rate hike.

“Banks have been building an anticipated hike into the rates they offer on fixed-term savings accounts for several months now,” says Katie Horne at the savings platform Flagstone. “A single 0.25% base rate increase isn’t expected to move fixed rates much further.”

At the time of writing, account puts it on a par with the top-paying fixed-rate savings accounts over two and three years.

The new account can be opened at a branch, online and via Nationwide’s app.

But as it involves locking away your money for two-and-a-half years, this needs to be cash that you won’t need for a while. Once the bond is open, you cannot access your money until the end of the term. For money that you might need to get your hands on, an instant access account or similar would be better.

You can only pay in money during the first 14 days after you open the account, and it is limited to one per saver. To apply, you must be 16-plus and have had a qualifying Nationwide or Virgin Money account since at least 2 November this year.

title: Reform UK councillor promoted collapsed $1.9bn ‘Ponzi scheme’ HyperVerse that left victims suicidal
author: Ben Quinn and Sarah Martin
text:
Susan Lawrence, elected to Wolverhampton city council, sits on committee overseeing financial reporting of multimillion-pound budget

A woman who promoted a notorious cryptocurrency scam has been elected as a Reform UK councillor and now sits on the audit and risk committee of a major city council.

Susan Lawrence was one of the main UK promoters of the HyperVerse cryptocurrency scheme, which was named in US court documents as an alleged “pyramid and Ponzi scheme” that cheated investors worldwide out of a “staggering” $1.89bn (£1.41bn).

The HyperVerse scheme spread through the US and the UK from 2020 to 2022, and also targeted investors in developing countries across Asia, Africa and the Pacific before its eventual collapse left many people unable to access funds.

In some cases, people who took out bank loans to buy packages in the scheme said they felt suicidal when they were unable to withdraw their money, with some cases of self-harm.

Lawrence is now a Reform councillor on Wolverhampton city council and sits on the authority’s audit and risk committee, which independently reviews governance and risk management and oversees the financial reporting relating to a multimillion-pound budget.

Lawrence, who has not personally been accused of wrongdoing by authorities, promoted the HyperVerse scheme, or later variations of it, even after the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) issued a consumer warning that the firm may have been promoting financial services or products without the regulator’s permission.

“You should avoid dealing with this firm and beware of scams,” the FCA said in a 2021 warning.

In a 2022 presentation, Lawrence addressed members of the HyperVerse community who were concerned they could no longer access their invested funds.

Lawrence, who worked with a fraudster whose company was later forcibly shut down by the UK high court, participated in lengthy promotional videos and webinars to market the project to the public and recruit new participants.

She is also linked to various other cryptocurrency schemes that were promoted by HyperVerse’s alleged co-founder Sam Lee, an Australian bitcoin entrepreneur who moved to Dubai in 2021.

Lee was charged in the US in 2024 with both civil and criminal offences for his role in the HyperVerse schemes. He has denied all charges.

Lawrence travelled to Dubai to meet Lee, and was filmed promoting two other related investment schemes. She was also referred to as a “super leader” for one of Lee’s investment platforms called “Vidilook”. The status of a group participant is usually based on how many other people they recruit into the scheme.

Lawrence continued to promote iterations of the same network, including one that was later subject to a cease and desist order by US federal authorities which described it as a “fraudulent pyramid and Ponzi scheme”. US authorities said: “It does not sell or purport to sell any actual product and has no apparent source of revenue other than funds received from investors.”

She promoted the Ponzi schemes alongside Desmond Amey, the scams’ key UK-based promoter. The UK’s high court acted to shut down the company used by him to funnel millions of pounds into the platforms.

Lawrence did not respond when approached by the Guardian. A spokesperson for Reform UK said: “Cllr Lawrence was one of many victims of this scam, losing her pension and tens of thousands of pounds on a scheme she believed was genuine.

“She later became involved with HyperNation in an attempt to recoup the money she had lost.

“She was not employed by Des Amey and has not been questioned by any authority over her links. Cllr Lawrence has no current involvement in any of these companies or any similar schemes.”

Reform, which has been under renewed pressure over its vetting processes amid new allegations about the conduct of councillors and candidates, did not respond to a question about whether its vetting team had picked up on Lawrence’s background.

title: Strait of Hormuz could reopen as part of Qatari plan for Iran nuclear inspections
author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
text:
Trump still considering new assault on Iran nuclear sites – though threats less credible after Vance remarks

Qatar, the lead mediator in the US-Iran conflict, is seeking to persuade Tehran to allow UN nuclear weapons inspectors to visit Iran’s bombed nuclear sites, including those housing the country’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

Iran would not be required to make any commitment that the stockpile would be removed from the country, with other options on the table, including reducing the uranium content by down-blending it.

Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, the emir of Qatar, spoke to Donald Trump about the proposal, the emir’s office said on Friday without revealing the call’s contents.

The state news agency said the emir “emphasised the importance of continuing dialogue and embracing diplomacy as a means of resolving disputes, preventing further escalation in the region”.

Trump is still considering whether to mount a further assault on Iranian nuclear sites, though the credibility of his threats is weaker inside Iran after his vice-president, JD Vance, said the war itself, and not just its cost to American consumers, was critical to the collapse of the Republican vote in the US midterms .

Under the Qatar proposal, the US would immediately lift the naval blockade on Iran in the strait of Hormuz and release a portion of the $8bn (£6bn) of its frozen assets. In return, Iran would agree to visits by International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to its bombed nuclear facilities, based on a previous abandoned agreement that had been reached in Cairo in September 2025.

Iran would open the strait of Hormuz on the second day, via a route it has already negotiated with Oman that they would jointly lodge with the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).

Iran has multiple other preconditions for opening the strait including ending the war in Lebanon, a withdrawal of US forces from the Iranian coastline, a commitment to lift some economic sanctions, and agreement to pay war reparations. The sequencing of these commitments has been at the heart of the mediation.

In the memorandum of understanding, a $300bn reconstruction and development fund was to be set up to help Iran recover economically, but it was never clear exactly how this proposal was to be funded.

Iran, in a triumphalist mood after Trump’s election wipeout, has been wary of allowing the UN nuclear inspectors back into the country, claiming it had lost faith in Rafael Grossi, the head of the inspectorate.

Tehran claims Grossi betrayed his duty to uphold the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, by failing to criticise the US for bombing Iran’s nuclear sites. It fears that material gathered by the inspectors would be handed over as targeting data to the Americans and Israelis.

In the parallel talks on opening the strait, Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, spoke again to Iran about the future of the strait administration including the agreed route, the extent to which the agreement is temporary and the need to register the proposal with the IMO, either as a bilateral agreement or a joint regional proposal.

Oman has a long-term proposal for the administration of the strait compliant with the law of the sea in that shipping companies would be charged only for services, and not tolls.

Amir Hayat Moqaddam, the deputy chair of the Iranian parliament’s national security and foreign policy committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA) on Tuesday that ships from four countries – China, India, Qatar and Iraq – were allowed to pass through the strategic waterway.

The exemptions served mutual interests, he said, adding that Iran charged Indian and Chinese vessels transit fees while allowing Qatari ships to pass free of charge. Medicine was received from India, while China provided political support.

It is reported that of the 10.23m barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42% went to China and 13% to India, said Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler.

The navy of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said two “violating” oil tankers attempting to pass through an unauthorised route in the eastern sector of the strait of Hormuz had collided with mines and caught fire.

The IRGC said the two tankers had turned off their navigation and identification systems and that the attempted crossing was with the support of US military forces.

title: Can we play you every week? The day Southend toppled Man United
text:
Twenty years ago, Southend United sent shockwaves through English football as they dumped Manchester United out of the Carling Cup.

A stunning 30-yard free-kick from Freddy Eastwood clinched victory over Sir Alex Ferguson's star-studded side featuring Cristiano Ronaldo and Wayne Rooney, who were top of the Premier League.

It sparked elation both in the stands and on the pitch at Roots Hall as the struggling Shrimpers, who were bottom of the Championship, progressed to the quarter-finals.

Those involved in Southend's fairytale cup run have relived the club's finest hour with BBC Essex in a four-part podcast .

It was billed as an irresistible David v Goliath match-up: Lowly Southend against the world famous Manchester United in the fourth round of the cup.

Sir Alex made nine changes but still fielded 10 internationals in an attempt to avoid slipping up, with 11,532 fans cramming into Roots Hall to see a potential upset.

Darren Fletcher, Alan Smith and Gabriel Heinze were among the stars to play alongside Ronaldo and Rooney in what was a £58.75m line-up.

"We saw the teamsheet and you do fear the worst," admits Steve Tilson, who was Southend manager on the night.

Goalkeeper Darryl Flahavan recalls first learning of the Red Devils' starting 11 over the stadium's loudspeaker.

"I always remember my goalkeeping coach at the time, Lee Turner, coming up to me and just whispering in my ear, 'I think you're going to be busy tonight, mate'," he says.

Yet despite the odds stacked in their favour, Jon Champion, who commentated on the game, recalls Sir Alex's men looking uncomfortable at the old-school Roots Hall.

"I remember looking at some of them - who'd clearly never seen anything quite like this before in their football careers - and they did look like fish out of water," he says.

Buoyed by an electric atmosphere near the seaside, the side with nothing to lose made a fierce start.

When Jamal Campbell-Ryce was fouled 30 yards from goal in the 27th minute, history was about to be made.

Boyhood United fan Freddy Eastwood had twice before trialled for the Red Devils. He stood over the free-kick with Steven Hammell.

"I said to Stevie just before I hit the ball, 'No, I'm taking it because I'm going to score'," Eastwood reminisces.

Southend's top-scorer arrowed the ball past the Manchester United wall and into the top corner.

"There was just an explosion of noise as the net rippled," Champion says.

"It was a dawning realisation that a very special moment was unfolding."

For Tilson, it began an agonising wait for the full-time whistle: "You look at your watch and you think, 'It's a long time to go. Are we going to be able to hold on?'."

United responded with force, but heroics from Flahavan to twice deny Ronaldo - who went on to be crowned the world's best footballer five times - helped to keep the Old Trafford side at bay.

"I knew it was going to be a big night for me and a night I wanted to do myself justice," Flahavan says.

Eastwood adds: "Ronaldo was everywhere, he was shooting from everywhere – they just didn't get the goal."

"The longer the game goes on and you get down to the last five minutes, you hope and pray you can pull it off," says Tilson.

Referee Uriah Rennie's final whistle prompted scenes of jubilation inside Roots Hall as the home side won 1-0 .

Among the overjoyed fans was legendary singer Alison Moyet, who, such was the high demand, had called in a favour from Tilson for a ticket after he recently watched her perform.

The Southend Echo reported selling a record-breaking number of newspapers the next day, leading to it being reprinted.

Journalists from the nation's media had all desperately pursued the man at the centre of it all for an interview.

"I was getting chased all over the place, I don't think I even went home that night," Eastwood remembers.

"We had a night out the night after and celebrated it properly, because after the game we just couldn't get out the stadium.

"There were so many fans, everyone was so full of joy."

Southend were to continue wrestling against the Premier League elite, as they drew Tottenham Hotspur at White Hart Lane in the quarter-final.

The establishment-defying Shrimpers took Spurs to extra-time and came within five minutes of a penalty shootout, but for a winning Jermain Defoe goal.

Manchester United, meanwhile, went on to win the Premier League and reach the semi-finals of the Champions League.

Tilson, of course, will never forget what his team did against that great side.

"It wasn't a case of we were hanging on for 90 minutes," he insists.

"We played some good football and I thought we thoroughly deserved the win in the end."

title: The PM’s small measures aim to help the public take back control – and we know how powerful that can be | Gaby Hinsliff
author: Gaby Hinsliff
text:
E-bikes, noisy headphones, flytipping: Burnham is weighing in on areas that make a difference to how people feel about life

I magine waking up one morning to find a humiliating video of you, filmed without your knowledge or control, plastered all over social media. Maybe you were sweating at the gym; or maybe at work, in a bar, or walking down the street, where you never realised the stranger hassling you for your number was covertly filming for his social media channel dedicated to shaming women who won’t date him.

This week ministers hinted at a potential crackdown on so-called pervert glasses , wifi-enabled spectacles that let the wearer capture video of people around them, after multiple reports of men using them to harass women. (Though a small flashing light on the frame is meant to warn that the user is filming, it’s easily missed and worryingly easily disabled.) If so, it would be a small win, admittedly, in the context of what feels like an endless losing battle against big tech. But it would give young women back some small sense of control in life, and that matters perhaps more than we think.

When Andy Burnham declared war last month on people listening to loud music on the bus without headphones, he was mocked for fiddling while Rome burns. What next, jail time for finishing off the milk and putting the empty carton carefully back in the fridge? But if anything, the prime minister has since doubled down on sweating the small stuff. In a week in which unknown forces have been disrupting food supplies and grounding flights across Europe, Burnham found time to weigh in personally over thoughtless idiots abandoning hire bikes in the middle of city pavements – a genuine problem for blind people and people trying to get round them with pushchairs or wheelchairs, but usually the sort of crackdown left to junior ministers – and on the attempt to save Poundland shops for the nation . It wasn’t until I spoke to the former Starmer strategist Claire Ainsley about her new book, Control: How We Lost it and How to Take it Back , that something clicked into place: all these policies are about exerting control, in situations where we feel it’s been taken away from us.

In the book, she writes that the classic advice given to people in anxious times is to focus on what you can do – small things over which everyone has mastery – and worry about the rest later, when you can ideally tackle it in a calmer frame of mind. And that’s essentially how Burnham is approaching Britain, an anxious country with much to be anxious about currently. There may be little its prime minister can realistically do about Donald Trump (that’s one for American voters, who made a promising start this week), Vladimir Putin, oil prices or a stock market slump that may or may not herald the beginning of the AI bubble bursting. But combating small acts of selfishness, that make a surprisingly big subliminal difference to how people feel about their lives, their high streets, the public realm through which they move, are very much in his wheelhouse.

The freedom to just unlock a Lime bike and cycle away undoubtedly changed city life for the better, but with it came a whiff of anarchy. Hire bike riders have earned their reputation for jumping red lights, zooming along pavements, knocking over pedestrians and abandoning their bikes wherever it suits them when they’re done. But transport secretary Heidi Alexander’s consultation will also look at illegal and antisocial riding, picking up on persistent reports from outside big cities of something darker and more intimidating; packs of balaclava-wearing young men burning through housing estates on dirt bikes and e-scooters that aren’t legal on roads, yelling abuse at anyone trying to stop them, fuelling a sense that the police have lost control of the neighbourhood. This kind of antisocial behaviour isn’t new – 20 years ago it was teenage joyriders stealing cars – but when it leaves parents feeling it’s not safe to take their kids to the park, it’s corrosive on a much deeper level. In parliament recently, the Darlington MP Lola McEvoy described illegal e-bike rider s running amok in her constituency as a “visible degradation of our collective social contract”.

The summer’s crackdown on fly-tipping , again personally fronted by the prime minister, fits a similar pattern: his new Makerfield constituency was home for years to an illegal dump full of rotting, rat-infested rubbish that despite his best efforts the previous MP Josh Simons couldn’t get anyone in authority to shift, until it caught fire and a nearby primary school had to close . In her book, Ainsley quotes Simons describing the first year in office for many new Labour MPs as “a crash course in state failure”.

If all Andy Burnham can ultimately offer the country is petty crackdowns while the world goes to hell in a handcart, then his project is doomed to fail. (Keir Starmer used to talk before the last election about small steps to win back the confidence of voters angry with politicians, and look what happened to him.) But “take back control” was a powerful slogan for Vote Leave for good reason. If Labour could somehow creatively reinterpret it to mean a country where the state actually works, big tech can no longer operate with no thought for the human consequences, predators don’t have licence to behave as they please and pensioners have a fighting chance of making it down a pavement – well, isn’t that what we used to call governing?

title: The end of Maga as we know it
author: David Smith in Round Rock, Texas
text:
The Republican party will regroup after their shellacking in the US midterm elections, but it won’t look the same

Walking by a tattoo studio and medical spa on the pretty main street of Round Rock , in Texas Hill Country, Tarik Bakir recalled voting for Barack Obama in 2008 and Donald Trump in 2024. But when it came to the 2026 midterm elections, he was firmly back in the Democrats’ column.

“I’m not happy with the Iran war,” said Bakir, 41, a financial adviser who served with the US military in Afghanistan. “The economy’s OK , but not great. This election was a rebuttal to Trump. This time people said they didn’t like him, or his policies.”

Once a reliably Republican suburb north of Austin, Round Rock is the birthplace of James Talarico, whose victory this week in a US Senate election – Democrats’ first in Texas since 1988, the year before Talarico was born – symbolised a nationwide “blue-nami” that swept away Trump’s Maga (Make America Great Again) coalition.

It was the most sweeping midterm repudiation of a sitting president since the Watergate election of 1974. Unlike typical midterms, where losses are concentrated in swing districts or isolated suburban pockets, the 2026 midterms saw the Republican floor drop out across deep-red strongholds, suburban corridors and rural heartlands alike.

Democrats stormed once impregnable fortresses such as Kansas and South Carolina, taking control of both chambers of Congress and redrawing the political map. In Texas, for decades a bedrock of conservatism, the senator Ted Cruz is now the last statewide Republican still standing.

For Trump, it was a scathing rebuke after a madcap campaign that left some wondering: if the president had deliberately tried to sabotage his own party’s chances, what, precisely, would he have done any differently?

The president heaped praise on Ohio senator Jon Husted’s “ass” but, in the words of Cruz, his party got an “ass-kicking”. Florida governor Ron DeSantis called it “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country”.

Patrick Gaspard, a former official in Barack Obama’s White House, said: “Anyone who says that they were not surprised is lying. This busted all of the models across all demographics and geography. You would think that 2024 was the last century, not just two years ago.”

Why did Maga fall apart so fast , and in such colossal fashion? The short answer is that costs, corruption and conflict with Iran left Trump supporters feeling betrayed.

Frank Luntz, a veteran pollster and strategist, hosted a focus group on the eve of the election with people who voted for Trump in 2024 , but would be voting for Democrats in 2026.

Affordability issues were “hurting Trump voters more than others because they are more likely to be paycheck-to-paycheck voters”, said Luntz. “They are more likely to have no money at the end of the week , and very little money at the end of the month , and so they were susceptible to food and fuel prices more than the average voter.”

“They were promised in 2024 that prices would come down, and we wouldn’t have forever wars, that we would drain the swamp,” Luntz added. “They looked in 2026 and they felt not nearly enough had been accomplished on this and so they wanted to punish Republicans . This is not about rewarding Democrats. This was about holding Republicans accountable for these voters believing what they were promised.”

Instead of focusing on the economic pressures hurting many of his own supporters, like farmers struggling to pay for diesel and fertiliser, Trump diverted his public commentary towards vanity projects, legal grievances and high-profile spats.

“He lost the plot,” according to Luntz. “He was talking about topics that they didn’t fully understand and didn’t care about. He wasn’t talking about the things that mattered most to them and in the end they took it out on the Republican party.”

Gaspard , a distinguished senior fellow at the Center for American Progress thinktank in Washington, agrees that the Maga coalition fractured because Trump violated every pledge made to working-class voters – from sweeping tariffs on foreign goods and an unpopular military conflict in Iran to cryptocurrency self-enrichment schemes and federal immigration overreach that terrorised local communities.

The result has broken the psychological chokehold Trump exerted over his party, Gaspard believes. “We’re seeing it already. When your approval hits the low 30s , politicians think about survival,” he said. “What happened creates a permission structure finally for Republicans to develop a spine to move away from him on their political choices, their policy choices and how they navigate their cultural choices as well.”

He added: “Donald Trump can’t act as if he wasn’t present at the scene of the crime. He personally picked the candidates in Texas and South Carolina . His fingerprints are all around it , and he can’t proclaim his innocence.”

Republicans lost most of Trump’s gains with Latino voters in 2024, according to an Associated Press voter poll , while only about one in 10 Black men voted Republican in their local House race, down from roughly one in four who backed Trump in 2024. Voters under 30, who had been roughly evenly divided between Trump and Kamala Harris two years ago, backed Democratic House candidates by about seven-to-three this time.

Gaspard noted that the collapse extended to Trump’s prized demographic strongholds: “When you end up in an election where the Republican party ended up splitting men 50/50 with Democrats, that is a death knell for the manosphere , the bro platforms that they saw as their firewalls.”…

title: US midterm results may help unite Israeli coalition to unseat Netanyahu
author: Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem
text:
Democrats’ sweep could urge Israel’s divided opposition to join forces and remove prime minister closely allied with Trump

The Democrats’ sweep of Congress may make it easier for Israel’s splintered opposition to overcome deep internal divisions and form a coalition government, by increasing the urgency of unseating Benjamin Netanyahu, who has associated himself so closely with Donald Trump’s Republicans.

But as Israel took stock of the results, there was also a sense that the elections marked a longer-term shift in US politics that will make the job of any new Israeli leader far more difficult.

The United States provides Israel with critical military and diplomatic support, so nurturing bipartisan ties was the cornerstone of foreign policy for decades. Netanyahu ripped up that commitment to throw his lot in with the Republicans in general and Trump in particular.

The opposition had always attacked his decision as ill-judged. By the end of the week, they were warning that it was positively dangerous.

“These people aren’t against Israel,” prominent opposition politician Yair Lapid said of incoming Democratic lawmakers, urging his country to rebuild bridges. “They’re mainly against Netanyahu – for them, anything connected to him is toxic.”

“The easiest thing is to scream that ‘America is lost,’ because if it’s lost, you don’t have to work. That’s just not true. Not at all.”

Lapid laid out a plan to “rebuild trust” in the US, but it perhaps did more to demonstrate the scale of the problem than reassure Israelis.

His proposal of a transatlantic charm offensive by officials of a prospective new government drew a swift and sharp rebuke from the New York congressman-elect Brad Lander.

Lander, a Democrat who is Jewish and describes himself as a liberal Zionist, was detained in the occupied West Bank last month while joining Palestinians trying to harvest olives.

“Minister Lapid: As someone who won a seat in Congress last night, and who cares about Israel: you’re not listening to what American voters – Jewish and non-Jewish – are saying,” Lander wrote in a direct response.

“We aren’t starving for a barnstorming tour. We’re hungry to see respect for international law and human rights.”

In his exchange with Lapid, Lander also highlighted the arrest of journalist Abed Abu Shehada, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, as an example of how Israel violates international law. He drew a direct link with the ICE “regime of detention without charges, based on secret evidence, designed to intimidate and chill speech” that he said was rejected by US voters.

Abu Shehada was reportedly taken from his home by 15 masked security officials in a night-time raid, without an arrest warrant. Interrogators have only questioned him about a podcast interview with a public figure, lawyers acting for Abu Shehada said.

On Friday, Lander and two other incoming Jewish members of Congress, Daniel Bliss and Scott Wiener, wrote to Israel’s ambassador to the US calling for the immediate release of Abu Shehada.

“Detaining a reporter for conducting an interview — the only issue that interrogators questioned him about — is a violation of international law,” Lander said when he published the letter. “It comes at a time when senior Israeli officials are trying to delegitimize the participation of Palestinian citizens in Israel’s recent elections.”

Nor do Israel’s problems end with angry Democrats. The wounded Republican establishment lost no time looking a few thousand miles away to find reasons for the collapse of its voter base.

Soon after the election results came in, the vice-president, JD Vance, put “our relationship with Israel” on a short list of reasons for voter fury, and on election day Trump made a last-ditch attempt to woo voters with a pledge to cut off $4bn (£3bn) in annual military aid to Israel.

The announcement caused panic in Israel’s defence establishment. “When the commander of the Israel air force hears something like that, he might slit his wrists,” one official told Channel 12 news. “Where are we going to come up with 15 billion shekels every year, and what does that mean for Israel’s future defence budget?”

Netanyahu only responded to Trump’s electioneering on Friday with an attempt to spin the cut as a joint decision reflecting Israel’s economic strength. It demonstrated a “move from aid to partnership”, his office said in a statement.

Netanyahu has long flaunted his relationship with Trump, his fluent English and experience in the US, presenting himself as the only man with the international standing to guarantee Israel’s security in a hostile world.

After Tuesday’s US election, he looks more like an agent of its destruction to many in Israel. “One thing is clear: we are losing America,” Ben Caspit wrote in Ma’ariv, a daily newspaper.

“This isn’t a process; it isn’t happening in stages; it is happening all at once. It is an avalanche. It is a reverberating collapse of the foundation of Israel’s national defence doctrine. This isn’t a decree of fate. It is a decree of Netanyahu.”

Some advocates for change inside Israel found cause for hope in the Democrats’ victory, if Israel’s opposition can turn their mandate for change into a new government. They won 67 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, but more than a quarter went to Palestinian citizens of Israel, and some of the Jewish Israeli opposition parties have ruled out sitting with them.

title: What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?
author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya, Turkey
text:
Its key temperature goal has been missed but experts say the agreement is still proving a vital moral compass for progress

It was a curious way of conducting negotiations. Ahead of the 2025 climate summit, in the Amazonian port of Belém last year, the Brazilian hosts had taken off the table the issue that most had assumed would be at its heart: concrete plans from each country laying out exactly what they would be doing to cut their greenhouse gas emissions.

Brazil was insisting, instead, that these plans – the bedrock of the Paris agreement – were the business of national governments and not up for negotiation. “In that case, it will be a very short Cop,” one seasoned global south negotiator told the Guardian shortly before, reflecting a widespread unease. “There is nothing to negotiate.”

“They have decided that there is no appetite for negotiation, with the US out of Paris,” said another developing country diplomat. “Countries won’t engage.”

The summit ended with a deal, although few loved it. But, as the faultlines from the Brazilian decision deepen going into this year’s summit, it is clear that the Paris agreement, and climate action around the world, has reached an impasse.

And it is not just Cop insiders who are worried. For many outside the vast white air-conditioned conference halls, the question, as this year’s summit begins, will be: what is the point?

Those same governments have pledged year after year since the Paris agreement was signed in 2015 – and entered into force a year later – to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. Yet temperatures for two years have exceeded that threshold, and the UN revealed a few weeks ago that its most optimistic estimate was now for about 1.7 to 1.8C of heating .

There could be no clearer evidence that the Paris agreement, on the face of it, has failed. It is impossible not to wonder whether the Cop process itself is just not fit for purpose.

The charge sheet against Paris is long, with the central issue being the failure to achieve its goal. Beyond that immediate failure, the negotiation processes are endlessly convoluted and cause their own problems. It took more than five years just to negotiate the Paris “rulebook” under which the treaty is interpreted and put into effect.

The convention that all resolutions must pass by consensus has given bad actors free rein. Donald Trump’s allies – in Saudi Arabia, Russia, Venezuela and some other petrostates – frequently veto measures and obstruct progress .

It took more than 30 years of negotiation since the UN framework convention on climate change was signed in 1992 for fossil fuels even to be addressed directly. This was at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023, where countries agreed for the first time to “transition away from fossil fuels” but failed to set a timeframe or any policies to back up the resolution.

The US, the world’s biggest economy and responsible for about one in every eight tonnes of carbon dioxide emitted today, has withdrawn from Paris under President Trump.

Even parts of the developed world which support the process have mostly failed to come up with convincing plans: Australia, co-host of Cop31, has set no end to fossil fuel exports; its fellow co-host Turkey plans to increase its carbon output. The UK is opening a gasfield and mulling a new oilfield, Germany has dropped its electric vehicle sales targets and scrapped a renewable heating law. Meanwhile, most rich countries are reducing their contributions to climate finance for the poor.

Most of all, the slow pace of the Paris timetable might have seemed fine in 2015, when temperatures were rising at 0.2C a decade. Today, the rate of rise is 0.4C a decade and still accelerating.

“The structures of Cops and Paris are labyrinthine, bureaucratic, and ultimately dispiriting,” said Paul Bledsoe, a former Clinton White House climate adviser, now with the American University. “It may be time to streamline them to focus more deliberately on national emissions reduction goals.”

As ordinary people watch these failures outside and inside the process, some are losing faith. The Paris agreement was a sensation, celebrated around the world. In the years since, the aura of Cop has faded, as meetings seem to disintegrate into arguments over wording and compromise.

“A lot of the commitments, the promises that were made, just turned out to be a bunch of hot air,” said Juan Carlos Monterrey, former climate envoy for Panama, now chief executive of the Vanglabs consultancy. “Under that measure, we have failed.”

Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said: “The fact that global warming is accelerating, that we inevitably will be breaching the 1.5C limit within three to five years, that tipping points are coming closer fast, that Earth’s resilience is showing worrying signs of decline, and that we still allow ourselves to follow a global path that will take us to a catastrophic 2.6C-3C, and that this is allowed to happen within the framework of the Paris agreement, cannot be considered as anything but a global failure.”

But, like most involved in international climate efforts, both refuse to concede that Paris is done for. “On the other hand,” said Rockström, “Paris is all we have. And we know that the global climate crisis can only, in the end, be solved if all countries in the world simultaneously move away from planet-damaging heat injection.”

Monterrey agrees. The most important fact about the Paris agreement, and the Cop process, he says, is that they exist. “Paris is our moral compass. It has told us where we should go. The speed of travel is not what it needs to be, but Paris has set the direction.”

This year’s Cop is the first to have a split presidency and host. Being held in Turkey but presided over by Australia, Cop31 is a messy compromise between two countries whose other chief point of commonality is an admiration for coal.…

SABR : The Yankees’ Cody Bellinger was already awarded his second career Gold Glove for his excellent work in left field in 2026, but now he’s taken home an even higher honor. Since 2011, Rawlings has also given out one Platinum Glove per league each year to honor the best of the best. Now, they have two, as Bellinger was named the AL’s best defender, joining the truly outstanding Pete Crow-Armstrong, the NL winner and likely MVP. Congrats to Cody!

MLB.com | Bryan Hoch : Elite pitching, lackluster bats; such was the story of the 2026 Yankees. If the 2027 squad is to progress further into the postseason, offensive upgrades are a must. Here, Hoch examines a number of positions where the Bombers should seek more thump. To my eyes, the position that is most in need is also the spot with the most intriguing option – third base, where Ryan McMahon stunk it up this past year, and where NPB slugger Teruaki Sato is seeking to make a splash in free agency. It’s been a hot minute since the Yankees acquired NPB talent, so I’m not sure how seriously the Yankees will participate in the Sato sweepstakes (especially if they’re unsure about his glovework at the hot corner), but a blogger can hope.

FanGraphs | Eric Longenhagen : If you want more info on Teruaki Sato, Eric Longenhagen has you covered. The FanGraphs lead prospect analyst covered Sato as part of his overview on notable players from the NPB and KBO, had this to say about the 2026 Central League Triple Crown winner - “Though Sato isn’t a five-tool superstar – he’s going to strike out a lot and play below-average defense – he should hit for enough power to be a productive, heart-of-the-order power hitter with 25-30 home runs.”

Another potential upgrade for the Yankees, albeit at second base, is Shugo Maki of the Yokohama BayStars, who expressed his desire to play stateside last offseason, though he hasn’t been officially posted yet. Says Longenhagen: “Maki projects as an everyday second baseman in the Brandon Lowe mold, and you could make a pretty good argument that his hit-tool stability (Maki has a single-digit miss rate against fastballs compared to Sato’s whopping 32 percent) makes him a superior “prospect” when compared to Sato.”

NJ.com | Bob Klapisch : With yet another postseason run cut short, Yankees fans are understandably frustrated with Brian Cashman. However, former Athletics GM Billy Beane of “Moneyball” fame considers Cashman to be “one of the best that’s ever done this job. Period.” While your mileage may vary on Cashman’s maneuvering in recent years, one must acknowledge that his overall body of work remains very impressive. If you’re up in arms about Hal Steinbrenner handing Cashman another extension, maybe Beane’s words can offer you some reassurance. Or not.

Lastly, in case you missed Madison’s column , the Yankees are down a key member of the 2026 coaching staff. Tanner Swanson has gained a reputation since being hired away from the Twins in 2020 as one of the best catching instructors in baseball. As noted above Trevino became a Platinum Glove winner under his watch, and most impressively, he’s helped transform Austin Wells from a guy who might not stick behind the plate into a legitimately great defensive catcher who was a Gold Glove finalist himself in 2026. But his contract was up, and he’ll be heading to the Pacific Northwest because new Mariners skipper Jason Kanzler offered the Seattle native a job as his bench coach. Best of luck to him — and to the Yankees on finding his replacement.

title: US carries out another round of ‘minor’ strikes on Iran, Trump says
author: Guardian staff and agencies
text:
The president’s announcement comes days after an earlier attack on Iran was made public, and as diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have accelerated

Donald Trump has said the US military on Friday carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran, targeting an air defence system, describing the action as “minor.”

Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway for oil shipments that has been disrupted since the beginning of the US war on Iran in February.

In an exchange with reporters on Friday, Trump said “they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five”.

The US military had previously reported carrying out what it described as “defensive” strikes on Monday , when explosions were heard on the islands of Qeshm and Hengam and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas.

Friday’s strikes are the first since Trump’s Republican party was dealt a stunning repudiation in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US.

The electoral setback was stoked in part by voter dissatisfaction with Trump’s execution of the Iran war and elevated fuel prices – a byproduct of the war that has affected nearly every part of the global economy.

In the days since, Trump has vacillated between threatening to “destroy” Iran and suggesting a resolution to the war is near.

Differences with Iran about its nuclear program remain the thorniest issue and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the war.

US Central Command, which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, announced in a post on X late Friday that the US was offering “a reward of up to $20m and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above”.

The post included a link to the state department’s Rewards for Justice program.

Trump noted earlier Friday in an exchange with reporters that mediators’ discussions with Iran continue.

“We are talking to Iran. We have been,” said Trump.

A flurry of diplomatic phone calls in recent days between leaders in the Gulf and beyond has been aimed at easing tensions in the region. Concerns have mounted over the possibility that Trump could still order the US military to carry out new strikes against Iran.

US defense secretary Pete Hegseth spoke on Friday with his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, about developments, according to the Qatari government. Qatar has been mediating between the US and Iran to end the war.

The Qatari government announced the call between the countries’ defence officials after confirming earlier that Trump and Qatar’s emir had a separate call to discuss efforts to de-escalate tensions.

The telephone call between Trump and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al Thani focused on international efforts to end tensions, according to a statement from the Qatari ruler’s media office.

title: Democrats blast Trump’s decision to make Stephen Miller his chief of staff as president defends picking loyal ‘MVP’ - as it happened
author: Robert Mackey, Shrai Popat, Anna Betts, Taz Ali and Adam Fulton
text:
Welcome to our live coverage of the US midterm elections – here are some of the latest key developments.

A number of closely watched contests in the midterms are still to be called, including the final two US Senate races – in Mississippi and Alaska. The Democratic candidates are hoping to oust Republican incumbents to bolster their new majority in Congress. Right now, Democrats have a 106-seat majority as we await final results.

Democrats flipped another eight House seats , strengthening their majority in the lower chamber. Democrats are now leading Republicans 253 to 157, with 25 races left to call, as a number of GOP representatives felt the weight of the blue wave that has swept their party out of power. Republicans held on to two House seats in the west as congressman Mike Kennedy won re-election in Utah and Amanda McKinney won in Washington.

Democratic socialist Nithya Raman was elected to serve as the mayor of Los Angeles , eking out a narrow win over incumbent Karen Bass, in a major shake-up in local politics that reflects the growing dissatisfaction with the direction of the city. The progressive urban planner had served on LA’s city council since 2020.

Harmeet Dhillon, a key Trump ally, resigned from her position leading the justice department’s Civil Rights division. Attorney general Todd Blanche said he accepted her notice. Dhillon is the first high-ranking justice department official to leave after the midterm elections. Democrats are expected to use their power in taking control of Congress to aggressively investigate executive agencies, including the justice department.

Abdul El-Sayed , the Democratic senator-elect in Michigan, said the new majority in the upper chamber needed “action” from their leader. On the campaign trail El-Sayed refused to back Senator Chuck Schumer, who currently serves as the minority leader. Speaking to CNN, El-Sayed reiterated that Senator Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat, would be an “amazing Senate majority leader”, but didn’t completely rule out supporting Schumer.

Joining the chorus of Republicans who blasted their party’s midterms performance is Senator Ted Cruz of Texas , who said the GOP were handed an “ass-kicking” in losing control of Congress. “It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election, it was a Watergate-level repudiation,” he said on his podcast.

The Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5% on Thursday amid growing signs the artificial intelligence industry will face tougher regulation because of the midterm results.

Donald Trump signed a proclamation that preserves the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as national monuments in his first official action after the Republican wipeout.

title: Ousted Paraguay president under house arrest after banking crisis leaves 60% of country unable to access accounts
author: Tiago Rogero South America correspondent
text:
Santiago Peña was detained minutes after he was impeached by Congress, as protesters took to the streets demanding answers after the suspension of the Ueno bank

Paraguay’s rightwing president has been placed under house arrest minutes after he was impeached by Congress, amid a severe crisis that left more than half the country’s population unable to access their bank accounts.

Santiago Peña is being investigated about allegations he used his political influence to favour a bank that expanded exponentially under his government and was suspended this week after irregularities .

The move froze the accounts of 2.9 million people, about 60% of the country’s adult population, who were customers of the bank – Ueno - and who overnight could no longer use their own money even for basic purchases such as bread and water.

Protests spread across the country, some involving violent clashes with police. Impeachment proceedings began on Wednesday before being concluded on Friday, minutes before Peña’s arrest was ordered.

His vice-president, Pedro Alliana, was being sworn in as the country’s new leader while a public prosecutor, accompanied by police outside Peña’s home, told local media the former president had been placed under house arrest.

“It has been established that he is indeed inside his home. He voluntarily allowed officers to enter and made himself available for all procedural purposes,” said prosecutor Elena Fiore Franco.

The public prosecutor’s office had opened an investigation into Peña on Thursday on suspicion of illicit enrichment, money laundering and influence peddling.

Peña, who was one of US president Donald Trump’s main allies in the region, had tried to resign on Thursday in an attempt to retain the special jurisdiction afforded to former presidents – who become senators for life in Paraguay – but lawmakers did not accept his resignation, leaving him subject to the ordinary courts.

Amid rumours he had fled to Argentina, the 47-year-old economist was expected to appear before Congress to present his defence during the impeachment proceedings, but left that to his lawyers and instead continued posting on social media.

Before the impeachment was concluded or the arrest warrant issued, he posted: “I say goodbye with gratitude, while fully recognising the anguish of those who are now waiting for answers,” referring to former Ueno customers who are unable to access their own money.

Soon after taking office, Peña appointed Carlos Carvallo Spalding, a former CEO of Ueno, head of the country’s central bank. Three months later, Spalding – who was by now regulating the company he used to run – allowed Ueno to become a digital bank, which put it on the path to becoming one of Paraguay’s largest banks by deposits in just a few years.

The arrest warrant for Peña also includes Spalding.

Peña himself had about US$1m in shares he bought in 2019 in a company that would become Ueno Holding in 2022, the parent company of the conglomerate that controlled Ueno Bank. Even after becoming president, he only disposed of the shares in April 2025. He said he had bought them purely as an “investor”.

As the bank aggressively expanded through an easy account-opening system and by promising returns far above those offered by the rest of the market, it also managed to bring public pension funds controlled by Peña’s administration into its portfolio.

“Because Ueno had the blessing of the presidency, most of the pension funds close to the government went to deposit their money in the bank,” said political analyst Hugo Duarte. An estimated $800m to $860m in state and pension funds were invested in Ueno.

As pressure mounted and retail sales fell by as much as 80% because much of the population could not access their own money, Peña lost the support of his own party.

During the impeachment session, opposition senator Rafael Filizzola said Paraguay was facing “one of the biggest corruption scandals since the return of democracy” and the “biggest fraud carried out from political power in the democratic era”.

title: 'My mortgage is going up £200': How rising interest rates are hitting people's pockets
text:
On Thursday, the Bank of England increased interest rates for the first time in over three years as it tries to get a grip on rising inflation linked to the Iran war.

Experts say there could be more hikes over the next 18 months, as the conflict continues to push up food, fuel and energy prices across the UK and worldwide.

Higher interest rates affect borrowing costs, however, which means mortgages, credit cards and personal loans could get more expensive for millions, even as savings rates improve.

For some, it could mean extra financial pressure at a time when they are already struggling with the cost of living. The BBC spoke to three people about how they could be affected.

Peter Gill, 48, is one of the around 1.3 million Britons on a variable rate mortgage.

These loans track the Bank of England base rate, with a margin on top determined by the lender, so any rise in interest rates can push up repayments.

Peter, who runs a small tiling business in Halifax, says his monthly repayments will go up by roughly £45 following Thursday's quarter-percentage point increase and he's worried they could climb higher.

But he still thinks it'd be more expensive to move onto a fixed-rate deal - which is when you pay a set amount of monthly interest for a period - and is prepared to stay put for now.

His higher mortgage costs come as the "cost of everything is going up", he says.

The father of two, who has a combined household income of £45,000 with his wife Faye, is having to pay his staff more because of increases in the national minimum wage. Raw material costs have also risen due to the war in Iran.

At home, the family's food, gas and electricity bills have gone up and he says he's working "about six and a half days a week" to shield them from the worst of it.

"From my point of view, inflation goes up which costs you, then interest rates go up and you have even less money."

Most UK mortgage holders are on fixed-rate deals, but that doesn't necessarily protect them when the Bank of England puts up rates.

David Hollingworth, from brokers L&C Mortgages, says many people will be shocked at how much higher fixed-rate deals are than they were five years ago following recent increases .

"Fixed rates have already risen due to market anticipation that interest rates would need to rise to combat higher inflation," he says.

Dawn Fazackerley-King is a Pilates instructor who lives near Ipswich and has previously spoken to the BBC about her struggles with the cost of living.

She was on a five-year fixed deal at 1.4%, which she took out in January 2022. But the mother of two is about to refix for two years and the best deal she can find is a 5.69% loan. That will push her costs up by about £200 a month.

"I don't know where that money is going to come from, it's something we are going to have to figure out as a family. It's stressful."

She and her husband, who have a joint income of about £70,000, have already gone through their direct debits and there's "no more obvious fat to trim".

There is also no scope for them to take on additional work, as they both work full time.

"We're still living in the same property, our household costs are remaining the same," Dawn says. "It's an additional cost of several hundred pounds but we're not getting anything extra for that."

When the Bank of England increases its base rate, credit card borrowing costs also tend to increase, although the impact is not always immediate.

It may affect people with outstanding debts, as providers can increase the interest rates they charge with 30 days' notice.

Ben Thomas, 41, from Shropshire, ditched his career as a chartered accountant during the Covid pandemic after a mental health crisis and retrained as a paramedic.

But the drop in income left him reliant on credit cards and personal loans for everyday living expenses and he is now £52,000 in debt.

Faisal Islam: How high will interest rates go?

Three ways the interest rate rise could affect you

Ben says he's reached an agreement to pause the interest on most of it, but he is still incurring charges on around £2,000 of credit card debt and is worried about his repayments going up.

"With all that's going on, rising interest rates is another cost to deal with," he tells the BBC.

As well as overall debt repayments of around £300 a month, he and his wife pay £760 on their mortgage. They have also struggled with higher food and energy bills.

Simon Trevethick is head of communications at StepChange, which has been helping Ben manage his debt. He says the debt charity has seen a 20% increase in people asking for support this year and warned of tougher times ahead.

"If higher borrowing costs feed through into household budgets over the coming months, we could see further pressure on people seeking support."

title: Stephen Miller, architect of Trump’s immigration crackdown, to become White House chief of staff
author: David Smith in Washington
text:
US president confirms Susie Wiles, current chief of staff and first woman to serve in the role, will step down

Stephen Miller, Donald Trump ’s most controversial aide and the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown, will become his new White House chief of staff days after Republicans lost control of the US Congress in US midterm elections.

The president announced the extraordinary appointment on Friday, confirming that Susie Wiles – his current chief of staff, and the first woman to serve in the role – had been ousted.

In a social media ‌post, Trump called Miller, 41, “one of ​my most trusted advisors” and praised Wiles for doing “an ⁠outstanding job”. Miller will begin on Monday.

Wiles, 69, reportedly handed in her resignation on Thursday night and said in a social media post that serving Trump “has been the honor of a lifetime”.

Holding an umbrella, Trump emerged from the White House South Portico on Friday for a trip to Florida. “I wanted to make a change,” he said. “I think Susie’s done a very good job ... Stephen’s been great, and we’ve got to make moves.”

“Stephen’s been with me from the beginning. He gets it,” the president said. “Very good politically and he’s a very good man. He’ll do a great job. Great manager.”

Trump then boarded the Marine One helicopter, followed by Miller, secretary of state Marco Rubio and close aide Natalie Harp.

In a statement, Wiles added: “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”

She said her commitment to “the President and the mission” will not change.

Miller’s appointment is the first sign of a shake-up at the White House following Republicans’ catastrophic defeat in the midterms. His record as a far-right firebrand implies that Trump is preparing for an aggressive fight against congressional Democrats’ oversight and investigations.

Chris Whipple, author of The Gatekeepers: How the White House Chiefs of Staff Define Every Presidency , told CNN: “It’s almost a declaration of war by Trump … He [Miller] only knows one gear and that’s full-throttle, full steam ahead over the cliff.”

David Axelrod, a veteran Democratic strategist, added on X : “For those who hoped the @POTUS might pivot to work with the incoming Congress, the appointment of Miller is a bucket of ICE cold water.”

Miller is one of the most polarising figures in the administration and one of Trump’s closest and longest-serving advisers, having joined his 2016 presidential campaign as a speechwriter. He is a former aide to the former senator Jeff Sessions of Alabama, who would go on to serve as Trump’s first attorney general.

In Trump’s first term, Miller was the driving force behind policies such as family separation and a travel ban on Muslim-majority countries. More than a hundred Democrats in Congress signed a letter to Trump calling Miller a “documented white nationalist” and demanding his removal.

A biography of Miller, written by journalist Jean Guerrero in 2020, was entitled Hatemonger.

Miller has served as deputy chief of staff since Trump’s return to the presidency in January 2025. He had been hugely influential in hardline immigration policies and demanding an end to birthright citizenship. He is also one Trump’s most ardent, outspoken and pugnacious defenders.

Appearing on Sean Hannity’s Fox News show on Monday, just before the midterms, Miller said of the president : “He saved America from a corrupt political class. He saved America from open borders. He saved America from countries that want the American way of life to end, from foreign adversaries, from domestic adversaries.”

Miller added: “President Trump took a bullet for you, he bled for you, he faced life in prison for you. And what he needs from you tomorrow is your vote.”

Wiles is the longest-serving White House chief of staff for Trump, who cycled through four of them during his first four-year term.

Wiles led Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign to victory and was credited with bringing discipline to a chaotic effort and clamping down on leaks from his second administration.

The Florida operative generally shunned the limelight. At Trump’s 2024 election night victory party, she repeatedly shook her head and avoided the microphone as Trump tried to coax her to speak to the crowd.

But Wiles made headlines last year when Vanity Fair magazine published a series of interviews with her and other top Trump administration officials. Her comments stood out for their candour, including her observation that Trump has an “alcoholic’s personality”.

Her departure came months after she indicated she no longer showed evidence of breast cancer after she underwent months of treatment for the disease. She went public with the diagnosis in March.

Critics said Miller’s appointment showed that Trump had learned the wrong lessons from Tuesday’s electoral reckoning.

Becca Balint, a Democratic congresswoman from Vermont, posted on X: “On Tuesday, the American people rose up and overwhelmingly voted in opposition to the disgusting and inhumane policies of this second Trump administration. What does Trump do? He promotes Stephen Miller – the architect of some of this administration’s worst decisions. Sickening.”

Anthony Scaramucci, who had a brief spell as White House communications director during Trump’s first term, tweeted : “Trump saw the midterm results and decided elevating Stephen Miller is the answer. 🤣 He is even more delusional than I thought. Or maybe he actually wants to finish destroying the @GOP? 🤔”

title: Ben Roberts-Smith collaborates with gym business run by influencer that sold ‘war crimes’ pre-workout supplement
author: Josh Butler
text:
Zero Limits supplements is co-owned by rightwing podcaster and fitness coach Chris Katelaris, also known as ‘Big Chocky’

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

Ben Roberts-Smith has collaborated with a gym supplements company run by a rightwing influencer which recently sold a pre-workout product called “war crimes”.

Roberts-Smith, one of Australia’s most decorated living soldiers who is currently awaiting trial on war crimes charges, has recently launched an apparel brand, Epic 1 Two, producing T-shirts and gym wear .

In October, he also appeared in a social media video collaboration between his brand and Zero Limits supplements, co-owned by the rightwing podcaster and fitness coach Chris Katelaris, also known as “Big Chocky”.

Roberts-Smith, Katelaris and others were filmed during a gym workout, with on-screen graphics reading “Zero Limits Supplements x Epic 1 Two”. Both brands were labelled “collaborators” on the video, which is also published on the Instagram grids of both brands.

Months earlier, Zero Limits had repeatedly posted online about a product titled “war crimes”, an energy supplement in the flavour “kill or capture cola”. Its label depicted a hooded captive on a chair in a room with an Australian flag on the wall, and a tall figure wearing a balaclava and military-style clothing.

In a video on 26 July, Katelaris promoted the product while holding a tub at the gym.

“You wanna drink out of a prosthetic leg? You wanna re-enact a Sparta kick? You wanna execute your workout?” he said.

“War crimes, it’s the pre-workout for you.”

Zero Limits, which says it is “veteran owned and operated”, does not currently list the “war crimes” product on its website, and Roberts-Smith is not shown endorsing, referencing or using that particular product.

The former soldier has praised another product from Zero Limits, posting an Instagram story – since shared by the brand – from Epic 1 Two’s Instagram page of himself drinking a separate pre-workout drink.

Roberts-Smith gave the brand a “massive shout out” and told followers to “get on their website and take a look”, sharing a link to its website. Roberts-Smith also last week appeared on the Zero Limits podcast, hosted by another founder of the supplements company of the same name.

Roberts-Smith was in April arrested and charged with five counts of war crime – murder , in relation to three incidents stemming from his service in Afghanistan in 2009 and 2012.

He has denied the charges, saying in a statement after his arrest : “As I’ve always maintained: I categorically deny all of these allegations … I will be taking this opportunity to finally clear my name. I’m proud of my service in Afghanistan.”

The three incidents allegedly involved Afghan nationals being shot dead by Roberts-Smith, or a subordinate under his command, while he was present, the AFP commissioner, Krissy Barrett, said in April.

Roberts-Smith was previously found in a defamation suit – using the civil standard of the balance of probabilities – to have murdered unarmed civilians while serving in the Australian Special Air Service Regiment (SAS) in Afghanistan.

The federal court found to the lower civil standard that Roberts-Smith kicked Afghan man Ali Jan in the chest, sending him falling backwards over a cliff before he landed on the ground. The court found that Roberts-Smith then ordered another soldier to shoot him dead.

Roberts-Smith was also accused in media reporting of shooting an unarmed prisoner who had a prosthetic leg . The leg was later used as a drinking vessel by soldiers.

Zero Limits, Katelaris and Roberts-Smith were contacted for comment.

In a statement via a lawyer, Zero Limits did not respond to specific questions, only answering: “The products are great, make sure you check them out.”

In a statement via the same lawyer, Katelaris also did not respond to specific questions, but said: “If you thought this was wild, wait until next week’s campaign drops.”

Katelaris lists himself as a “co-owner” of the supplements brand in his Instagram bio. He also promotes a range of merchandise under his own name in support of Roberts-Smith, including “I stand with BRS” T-shirts, hats, hoodies and stubby coolers.

title: Herta finally clears his last F1 superlicence hurdle
author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
text:
Colton Herta has cleared the final hurdles to qualifying for a Formula 1 superlicence with his penalty-free and productive Friday practice outing for Cadillac at the Brazilian Grand Prix.

Herta replaced Sergio Perez in FP1 at Interlagos, where he and Cadillac were seeking to seal the final point needed for Herta to be eligible for a superlicence.

He is a contender to race for the team next season but even if 2027 comes too soon getting a superlicence now would also make it much easier for Herta to remain an option in the years that follow, too.

A driver needs to accrue 40 superlicence points when applying for the first time. Cadillac thought this had already been achieved after his Mexico FP1 appearance a week ago, but Herta was still one short after a mix-up over a previous IndyCar result.

He was immediately back in the car for Brazil to seal the deal, though, so long as he completed 100km and did not get any penalty points on his licence in the session.

Herta could have been tripped up on either count. The red flag that emerged early in FP1 could have shortened running significantly enough that he did not do enough laps for it to count – and it also caused a brief scare when Herta went past the pit entry after the session had been red-flagged.

No action was taken as it was clear the red light panels came on too late for him to react and get into the pitlane.

Cadillac’s Marc Hynes said on Friday evening that the team wanted to be absolutely clear whether the 100km limit comes from total mileage or only mileage from timed laps, but either way Herta would be safe.

The Race understands the FIA is satisfied with what he did in FP1 so the superlicence point will be earned and his eligibility will be confirmed in due course.

Herta ran a full programme in FP1 with early laps on hard tyres hampered by some lock-ups before a switch to softs, which yielded a best lap 0.904s slower than Valtteri Bottas over one lap and 0.275s slower than the target Cadillac set him.

Herta was due to speak to media at the end of the day but withdrew from those activities as Cadillac said he was feeling unwell.

When Hynes spoke, though, he said Herta was making good progress with his F1 work dovetailed alongside a disappointing Formula 2 campaign in which he is only 19th in the standings.

"It was a huge step to come to Europe chasing the F1 dream, and I hugely admire that," Hynes said.

"F2 is difficult. You’ve got the guys that have come through in the same peer set from karting, they know all the tracks – you get very little mileage in F2 practice, they know the tyre very well, and the driving style is baked in. So to come into that is tough.

"FP1 is a good opportunity to get some mileage, and he’s got better every time. The nerves aren’t there that you have for the first one, and he’s really looking assured out there now."
